---
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:setting}
Let $(\Omega,\mathcal{F})$ be a measurable space carrying a filtration
$(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t\in\mathbb{N}_0}$, where $\mathbb{N}_0:=\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}$, with $\mathcal{F}_0=\{\emptyset,\Omega\}$
and $\mathcal{F}_\infty:=\sigma\left(\bigcup_{t\in\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{F}_t\right)\subseteq\mathcal{F}$, and let
$\mathbb{P}_0,\mathbb{P}_1$ be probability measures on $(\Omega,\mathcal{F})$, the \emph{null} and
the \emph{alternative}. Nothing is assumed about how the filtration arises. We
write $\mathcal{B}_{S}$ for the $\sigma$-algebra carried by a space $S$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:iid}
The \emph{i.i.d.\ model} generated by a pair $P_0,P_1$ of probability measures on
a measurable space $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{X}})$, the \emph{observation space}, is the
instance of \Cref{def:setting} in which
\[
   \Omega:=\mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{N}},\qquad
   X_n:\Omega\to\mathcal{X},\quad X_n(\omega):=\omega_n\ \ (n\in\mathbb{N}),
\]
$\mathcal{F}:=\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{X}}^{\otimes\mathbb{N}}$, $\mathcal{F}_t:=\sigma(X_1,\dots,X_t)$ and
$\mathbb{P}_i:=P_i^{\otimes\mathbb{N}}$. We call $P_0,P_1$ the \emph{one-observation} laws.
\Cref{def:setting} is in force throughout; the i.i.d.\ model is assumed only in
those statements that name it. A statement is therefore i.i.d.-only exactly when
the one-observation laws $P_0,P_1$ --- as opposed to the path measures
$\mathbb{P}_0,\mathbb{P}_1$ --- occur in it, and we say so as well.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- assumption-1: body_md -->
\label{ass:standing}
For every $t\in\mathbb{N}$, $\mathbb{P}_1\ll\mathbb{P}_0$ on $\mathcal{F}_t$ and
\[
   \mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}_1|_{\mathcal{F}_t}\,\big\|\,\mathbb{P}_0|_{\mathcal{F}_t}\right)\ <\ \infty ,
   \qquad\text{where}\qquad
   \mathrm{KL}(Q\|P):=\begin{cases}
      \mathbb{E}_{Q}\left[\log\frac{dQ}{dP}\right], & Q\ll P,\\
      +\infty, & \text{otherwise.}
   \end{cases}
\]
<!-- end assumption-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:one-obs}
In the i.i.d.\ model the chain rule gives
$\mathrm{KL}(\mathbb{P}_1|_{\mathcal{F}_t}\|\mathbb{P}_0|_{\mathcal{F}_t})=t\,\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)$, so
\Cref{ass:standing} says exactly
\[
   P_1\ll P_0\qquad\text{and}\qquad \mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)<\infty ,
\]
and we then write $R:=\frac{dP_1}{dP_0}:\mathcal{X}\to[0,\infty)$ for a fixed version of
the density, so that $\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)=\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[\log R]$ and $\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[R]=1$. Note
that the assumption is imposed at each \emph{finite} $t$ only: the path
divergence $\mathrm{KL}(\mathbb{P}_1|_{\mathcal{F}_t}\|\mathbb{P}_0|_{\mathcal{F}_t})$ diverges as $t\to\infty$
unless $P_0=P_1$, which is why every divergence between $P_0$ and $P_1$ below is
per observation, and every divergence in the general setting is per step and
conditional on the past.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:ratios}
Under \Cref{ass:standing} let
\[
   L_t:=\frac{d\mathbb{P}_1|_{\mathcal{F}_t}}{d\mathbb{P}_0|_{\mathcal{F}_t}}\qquad(t\in\mathbb{N}_0) ,
\]
a nonnegative $\mathbb{P}_0$-martingale with $L_0=1$, and define the \emph{one-step
ratio}
\[
   R_t:\Omega\to[0,\infty),\qquad
   R_t:=\frac{L_t}{L_{t-1}}\ \ \text{on }\left\{ L_{t-1}>0\right\} ,
   \qquad R_t:=1\ \ \text{elsewhere} .
\]
Because
$\mathbb{P}_1(L_{t-1}=0)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[L_{t-1}\mathbf 1_{\{L_{t-1}=0\}}]=0$, the
convention off $\left\{ L_{t-1}>0\right\}$ affects nothing asserted $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s. In the
i.i.d.\ model $L_t=\prod_{n\le t}R(X_n)$, and $R_t=R(X_t)$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.\ ---
but not $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s., since $\left\{ L_{t-1}=0\right\}$ may carry $\mathbb{P}_0$-mass. Every
identification below is therefore stated under $\mathbb{P}_1$.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:bayes}
Let $t\in\mathbb{N}$ and let $Y:\Omega\to[0,\infty]$ be $\mathcal{F}_t$-measurable. Then
\[
   \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}\left[ Y\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}\right]
   \ =\ \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}\left[ R_t\,Y\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}\right]
   \qquad\mathbb{P}_1\text{-a.s.}
\]
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
First, $L_t=0$ $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s.\ on $\left\{ L_{t-1}=0\right\}$: by the martingale property
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[L_t\mathbf 1_{\{L_{t-1}=0\}}]
=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[L_{t-1}\mathbf 1_{\{L_{t-1}=0\}}]=0$ and $L_t\ge0$. Hence
$L_{t-1}R_tY=L_tY$ $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s., both sides vanishing on
$\left\{ L_{t-1}=0\right\}$. Now let $A\in\mathcal{F}_{t-1}$. Using the density $L_{t-1}$ on
$\mathcal{F}_{t-1}$, then the pull-out property for the nonnegative
$\mathcal{F}_{t-1}$-measurable factor $\mathbf 1_AL_{t-1}$, then the identity just
proved, then the density $L_t$ on $\mathcal{F}_t$:
\[
   \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}\left[\mathbf 1_A\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[R_tY\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]\right]
   =\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}\left[\mathbf 1_AL_{t-1}R_tY\right]
   =\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}\left[\mathbf 1_AL_tY\right]
   =\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}\left[\mathbf 1_AY\right] .
\]
The variable $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[R_tY\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]$ is $\mathcal{F}_{t-1}$-measurable and
nonnegative, so this identity for every $A\in\mathcal{F}_{t-1}$ is the defining property
of $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[Y\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:evar}
In the i.i.d.\ model (\Cref{def:iid}), a map $E:\mathcal{X}\to[0,\infty]$ is an
\emph{\textsf{e}-variable{} for $P_0$} if it is
$\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{X}}$-measurable and
\[
   \mathbb{E}_{P_0}[E]\ \le\ 1 .
\]
We write
\[
   \mathcal{E}\ :=\ \left\{ E:\mathcal{X}\to[0,\infty]\ \text{measurable}\;\middle|\;\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[E]\le1\right\} .
\]
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{def:cond-evar}
Let $t\in\mathbb{N}$. A map $E_t:\Omega\to[0,\infty]$ is a \emph{conditional \textsf{e}-variable{} for
$\mathbb{P}_0$ at time $t$} if it is $\mathcal{F}_t$-measurable and
\[
   \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}\left[ E_t\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}\right]\ \le\ 1
   \qquad \mathbb{P}_0\text{-a.s.}
\]
A sequence $(E_t)_{t\in\mathbb{N}}$ of such maps is called a \emph{betting sequence}.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{def:wealth}
Given a betting sequence $(E_t)_{t\in\mathbb{N}}$, define
\[
   W:\mathbb{N}_0\times\Omega\to[0,\infty],\qquad
   W_0:=1,\qquad W_t:=\prod_{n=1}^{t}E_n .
\]
We call $(W_t)_{t\in\mathbb{N}_0}$ the \emph{test supermartingale{}} of the sequence
\cite{SSVV11,RGVS23}. In the i.i.d.\ model, when $E_t=E(X_t)$ for a single
$E\in\mathcal{E}$ and all $t$, we call $(W_t)_{t\in\mathbb{N}_0}$ the \emph{i.i.d.\ product} generated by
$E$ and write $W_t=W_t(E)$.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:supmg}
$(W_t)_{t\in\mathbb{N}_0}$ is a nonnegative $\mathbb{P}_0$-supermartingale with $W_0=1$, and
$E_t<\infty$ $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s.\ for every $t$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
$W_t=W_{t-1}E_t$ in $[0,\infty]$, with the convention $0\cdot\infty:=0$. Since
$W_{t-1}$ is nonnegative and $\mathcal{F}_{t-1}$-measurable, the pull-out property for
nonnegative extended-real variables gives
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[W_t\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]=W_{t-1}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[E_t\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]\le W_{t-1}$,
and induction from $W_0=1$ gives $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[W_t]\le1<\infty$. Finally
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[E_t\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]\le1$ forces $E_t<\infty$ $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label{def:reject}
Fix $\alpha\in(0,1)$ and put $\ell:=\log\frac1\alpha\in(0,\infty)$. The test
rejects at the \emph{rejection time}
\[
   \tau_\alpha:\Omega\to\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\},\qquad
   \tau_\alpha:=\inf\left\{ t\in\mathbb{N}\;\middle|\; W_t>\tfrac1\alpha\right\} ,
   \qquad \inf\emptyset:=\infty .
\]
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:typeI}
For every betting sequence and every $\alpha\in(0,1)$,
$\mathbb{P}_0(\tau_\alpha<\infty)\le\alpha$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
$(W_t)_{t\in\mathbb{N}_0}$ is a nonnegative $\mathbb{P}_0$-supermartingale with $W_0=1$, and
$\{\tau_\alpha<\infty\}=\{\sup_{t\in\mathbb{N}}W_t>\frac1\alpha\}
\subseteq\{\sup_{t\in\mathbb{N}_0}W_t\ge\frac1\alpha\}$. Apply Ville's
inequality \cite{Vil39}, \cite[Lem.~1]{How20} in the form of
\Cref{thm:app-ville}, with $x=\frac1\alpha$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
\label{def:typeII}
Fix $\alpha\in(0,1)$ and a betting sequence. Define
\begin{align}
   \gamma_\bullet(\alpha)&:\mathbb{N}_0\to[0,1], &
   \gamma_t(\alpha)&:=\mathbb{P}_1\left( W_t\le\tfrac1\alpha\right) ,
   \label{eq:gamma}\\
   \bar\gamma_\bullet(\alpha)&:\mathbb{N}_0\to[0,1], &
   \bar\gamma_t(\alpha)&:=\mathbb{P}_1\left(\tau_\alpha>t\right)
   =\mathbb{P}_1\left(\max_{0\le n\le t}W_n\le\tfrac1\alpha\right) .
   \label{eq:gammabar}
\end{align}
We call $\gamma_t$ the \emph{fixed-horizon} and $\bar\gamma_t$ the
\emph{sequential} type-II error.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:order}
$\bar\gamma_t(\alpha)\le\gamma_t(\alpha)$ for every $t\in\mathbb{N}_0$ and
$\alpha\in(0,1)$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
$\{\tau_\alpha>t\}=\bigcap_{n=0}^{t}\{W_n\le\frac1\alpha\}\subseteq
\{W_t\le\frac1\alpha\}$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:noinfty}
The type-I error is a single number because
$\mathbb{P}_0(\sup_{t}W_t>\frac1\alpha)\le\alpha$ involves a supremum over all
times. The formal analogue $\bar\gamma_\infty(\alpha)=\mathbb{P}_1(\tau_\alpha=\infty)$
carries no information for the sequences this paper is about: by
\Cref{prp:powerone} below it is $0$ for every i.i.d.\ product generated by an
$E\in\mathcal{E}$ of positive \textsf{e}-power{}. (For a general betting sequence it need not
vanish --- $E_t\equiv1$ gives $\tau_\alpha=\infty$ a.s.\ --- but then no
horizon-free statement is available either.) The type-II error is therefore
irreducibly a function of a horizon, and all statements below are indexed by
$t$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
\label{def:epower}
The \emph{\textsf{e}-power{}} of an $E\in\mathcal{E}$ \cite{VW21} is the quantity
\[
   \mathbb{E}_{P_1}\left[\log E\right]\ \in\ [-\infty,\infty] ,
\]
defined whenever $\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[(\log E)_+]<\infty$ or $\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[(\log E)_-]<\infty$.
Under \Cref{ass:standing} the positive part is always integrable
(\Cref{lem:epower-welldef}), so the \textsf{e}-power{} is a well-defined element of
$[-\infty,\infty)$ for every $E\in\mathcal{E}$.
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:nosymbol}
The \textsf{e}-power{} is written out as $\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[\log E]$ throughout rather than
abbreviated, and its conditional version, used in \Cref{sec:nfl}, as
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[\log E_t\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]$.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
\label{def:exponent}
For $E\in\mathcal{E}$ define
\[
   \Lambda_\bullet(E):[0,\infty)\to[-\infty,\infty],\qquad
   \Lambda_s(E):=-\log\mathbb{E}_{P_1}\left[ E^{-s}\right] ,
\]
and
\[
   \Lambda:\mathcal{E}\to[0,\infty],\qquad
   \Lambda(E):=\sup_{s\in[0,\infty)}\Lambda_s(E) .
\]
Note $\Lambda_0(E)=0$, so $\Lambda(E)\ge0$. We call $\Lambda_s(E)$ the
\emph{tilted exponent} at tilt $s$, and $\Lambda(E)$ the \emph{Chernoff--Stein
exponent of $E$}: it is the type-II error exponent that $E$ achieves in the
Chernoff--Stein regime --- level $\alpha$ fixed, horizon $t\to\infty$
(\Cref{prp:exponent}) --- and the classical Chernoff--Stein exponent
$\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$ is its supremum over the class, which is \Cref{thm:ceiling}. The
two levels of the name are related by exactly that theorem. At $E=R$ the value
is the Chernoff information of the pair (\Cref{cor:chernoffinfo}). The name
records the regime, not an identity: \Cref{prp:exponent} proves
$\Lambda(E)\le\liminf_t-\frac1t\log\gamma_t(\alpha)$ always, with equality under
a hypothesis; whether the inequality can be strict we do not know.
For a betting sequence with wealth
process $(W_t)_{t\in\mathbb{N}_0}$ define, in parallel, the \emph{$t$-step exponent}
\[
   \Lambda^{(t)}_\bullet:[0,\infty)\to[-\infty,\infty],\qquad
   \Lambda^{(t)}_s:=-\frac1t\log\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}\left[ W_t^{-s}\right]
   \qquad (t\in\mathbb{N}) ,
\]
and its optimised form
\[
   \Lambda^{(t)}:=\sup_{s\in[0,\infty)}\Lambda^{(t)}_s\ \in[0,\infty] .
\]
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:iidexp}
In the i.i.d.\ model, if $(W_t)_{t\in\mathbb{N}_0}$ is the i.i.d.\ product generated by a
single $E\in\mathcal{E}$, then
$\Lambda^{(t)}_s=\Lambda_s(E)$ for every $s\in[0,\infty)$ and every $t\in\mathbb{N}$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Under $\mathbb{P}_1=P_1^{\otimes\mathbb{N}}$ the factors $E(X_1),\dots,E(X_t)$ are
independent with common law that of $E$ under $P_1$. Moreover
$\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[E]\le1$ forces $P_0(E=\infty)=0$, hence $P_1(E=\infty)=0$ by
\Cref{ass:standing}, so $W_t^{-s}=\prod_{n\le t}E(X_n)^{-s}$ holds
$\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.\ (the identity can fail only where one factor is $0$ and another
$\infty$). Tonelli then gives
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[W_t^{-s}]=(\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[E^{-s}])^{t}$ in $(0,\infty]$; take
$-\frac1t\log$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:epower-welldef}
Under \Cref{ass:standing}, in the i.i.d.\ model, for every $E\in\mathcal{E}$,
\[
   \mathbb{E}_{P_1}\left[(\log E)_+\right]\ \le\ \mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)+1\ <\ \infty ,
   \qquad\text{and}\qquad
   \mathbb{E}_{P_1}[\log E]\ \le\ \mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0) ,
\]
with equality in the second bound if and only if $E=R$ $P_0$-a.s.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Young's inequality $xy\le x\log x-x+e^{y}$ holds for all $x\ge0$, $y\in\mathbb{R}$ (fix
$x$ and minimise the right-hand side over $y$). Since $\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[E]\le1$ gives
$P_0(E=\infty)=0$, we may apply it pointwise on the $P_0$-full set
$\{E<\infty\}$, with $x=R$ and $y=(\log E)_+\in\mathbb{R}$, and integrate against $P_0$:
\[
   \mathbb{E}_{P_0}\left[ R\,(\log E)_+\right]
   \ \le\ \mathbb{E}_{P_0}\left[ R\log R-R\right]+\mathbb{E}_{P_0}\left[ e^{(\log E)_+}\right] .
\]
The left side is $\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[(\log E)_+]$. On the right,
$\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[R\log R-R]=\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)-1$, and $e^{(\log E)_+}=\max(1,E)\le1+E$, so
$\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[e^{(\log E)_+}]\le1+\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[E]\le2$. Hence
$\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[(\log E)_+]\le(\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)-1)+2$, which is the first claim.
For the second, $\log$ is concave, so by Jensen's inequality applied to the
probability measure $P_1$ and the map $E/R$ (defined $P_1$-a.s.\ since $R>0$
$P_1$-a.s.),
\[
   \mathbb{E}_{P_1}[\log E]-\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)=\mathbb{E}_{P_1}\left[\log\tfrac ER\right]
   \le\log\mathbb{E}_{P_1}\left[\tfrac ER\right]=\log\mathbb{E}_{P_0}\left[ E\mathbf 1_{\{R>0\}}\right]\le0 .
\]
For the equality case, equality in Jensen's inequality for the strictly concave
$\log$ forces $E/R$ to be $P_1$-a.s.\ equal to a constant $c$, and equality in
the last step forces $\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[E\mathbf 1_{\{R>0\}}]=1$. On $\{R>0\}$ the
measures $P_0$ and $P_1$ are equivalent --- if $A\subseteq\{R>0\}$ has
$P_1(A)=\int_AR\,dP_0=0$ then $P_0(A)=0$ --- so $E=cR$ $P_0$-a.s.\ on
$\{R>0\}$, whence $1=\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[E\mathbf 1_{\{R>0\}}]=c\,\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[R]=c$. Finally
$\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[E]\le1=\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[E\mathbf 1_{\{R>0\}}]$ gives
$\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[E\mathbf 1_{\{R=0\}}]=0$, so $E=0=R$ $P_0$-a.s.\ there. Conversely
$E=R$ gives equality throughout.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{rem:two-scalars}
$\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[\log E]$ is a statement about the \emph{mean} of $\log E$;
$\Lambda(E)$ about its \emph{lower tail}. \Cref{sec:nfl} shows the first
bounds nothing on its own, and \Cref{sec:ceiling} determines the exact range of
the second.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:chernoff}
For every betting sequence, every $\alpha\in(0,1)$, every $s\in[0,\infty)$ and
every $t\in\mathbb{N}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:chernoff}
   \bar\gamma_t(\alpha)\ \le\ \gamma_t(\alpha)
   \ \le\ \exp\left( s\ell-t\,\Lambda^{(t)}_s\right) .
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Fix $s\in[0,\infty)$. Since $x\mapsto x^{-s}$ is nonincreasing on $[0,\infty]$
(with the conventions of \Cref{sec:setup}),
\[
   \left\{ W_t\le\tfrac1\alpha\right\}\subseteq\left\{ W_t^{-s}\ge\alpha^{s}\right\} ,
\]
so Markov's inequality applied to the nonnegative variable $W_t^{-s}$ gives
$\gamma_t(\alpha)\le\alpha^{-s}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[W_t^{-s}]
=\alpha^{-s}e^{-t\Lambda^{(t)}_s}$, and $\alpha^{-s}=e^{s\ell}$.
\Cref{lem:order} gives the first inequality.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prp:exponent}
Work in the i.i.d.\ model. Let $E\in\mathcal{E}$ and let $(W_t)_{t\in\mathbb{N}_0}$ be the
i.i.d.\ product generated by $E$. Then
\eqref{eq:chernoff} reads
$\bar\gamma_t(\alpha)\le\gamma_t(\alpha)\le\exp(s\ell-t\Lambda_s(E))$, so that
$\liminf_{t\to\infty}-\frac1t\log\gamma_t(\alpha)\ge\Lambda(E)$. If in
addition $\mathbb{E}_{P_1}|\log E|<\infty$, $\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[\log E]>0$, and $0$ lies in the interior
of $\left\{ x\in\mathbb{R}\;\middle|\; I(x)<\infty\right\}$, where $I:\mathbb{R}\to[0,\infty]$ is the Cram\'er rate
function of $\log E$ under $P_1$ (\Cref{thm:app-cramer}, from
\cite{Cra38}, \cite[Thm.~2.2.3]{DZ10}), then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cramerlimit}
   \lim_{t\to\infty}-\frac1t\log\gamma_t(\alpha)\ =\ \Lambda(E) .
\end{equation}
Statement \eqref{eq:cramerlimit} concerns the fixed-horizon error. For the
sequential error only the inequality
$\liminf_{t}-\frac1t\log\bar\gamma_t(\alpha)\ \ge\ \Lambda(E)$
is claimed here.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
The displayed bound is \Cref{lem:chernoff} combined with \Cref{lem:iidexp};
taking $-\frac1t\log$ and then the supremum over $s$ gives the $\liminf$
statement.

For \eqref{eq:cramerlimit}, write $Y_n:=\log E(X_n)$ for $n\in\mathbb{N}$, and put
$S_t:=\sum_{n\le t}Y_n$, $\bar Y_t:=t^{-1}S_t$ for $t\in\mathbb{N}$, so that
$\gamma_t(\alpha)=\mathbb{P}_1(S_t\le \ell)=\mathbb{P}_1(\bar Y_t\le \ell/t)$; let $I$ be the
Cram\'er rate function of $Y_1$ under $P_1$. We record three properties of $I$:
it is convex, it vanishes at $\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[Y_1]=\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[\log E]>0$, hence it is
nonincreasing on $(-\infty,\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[\log E]]$; and it is finite in a neighbourhood of
$0$, hence continuous at $0$, by the interiority hypothesis.

\emph{Upper bound on $\gamma_t$.} Fix $t_1\in\mathbb{N}$ with $\ell/t_1<\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[\log E]$. For
$t\ge t_1$ we have $\ell/t\le \ell/t_1$, so
$\{\bar Y_t\le \ell/t\}\subseteq\{\bar Y_t\in F\}$ with $F:=(-\infty,\ell/t_1]$
closed. Since $I$ is nonincreasing on $(-\infty,\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[\log E]]\supseteq F$,
$\inf_{x\in F}I(x)=I(\ell/t_1)$, so the large-deviation upper bound of
Cram\'er's theorem \cite{Cra38}, \cite[Thm.~2.2.3]{DZ10}
(\Cref{thm:app-cramer}) gives
\[
   \liminf_{t\to\infty}-\tfrac1t\log\gamma_t(\alpha)\ \ge\ I\left( \ell/t_1\right) .
\]

\emph{Lower bound on $\gamma_t$.} Since $\ell/t>0$, the open set
$G:=(-\infty,0)$ satisfies $\{\bar Y_t\in G\}\subseteq\{\bar Y_t\le \ell/t\}$, so
the large-deviation lower bound of \Cref{thm:app-cramer} gives
\[
   \limsup_{t\to\infty}-\tfrac1t\log\gamma_t(\alpha)\ \le\ \inf_{x<0}I(x)
   \ =\ \lim_{x\uparrow0}I(x)\ =\ I(0) ,
\]
the first equality by monotonicity of $I$ on $(-\infty,\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[\log E]]$ and the
second by continuity at $0$.

\emph{Conclusion.} Combining and then letting $t_1\to\infty$, so that
$I(\ell/t_1)\to I(0)$ by continuity, squeezes both outer quantities to $I(0)$.
Finally $I(0)=\sup_{\theta\in\mathbb{R}}\{-\log\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[e^{\theta\log E}]\}
=\sup_{s\ge0}\Lambda_s(E)=\Lambda(E)$: the substitution $\theta=-s$ turns
$\theta<0$ into $s>0$ and $-\log\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[e^{\theta\log E}]$ into
$\Lambda_s(E)$, while for $\theta>0$ Jensen gives
$\log\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[e^{\theta\log E}]\ge\theta\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[\log E]>0$, so positive $\theta$
contribute a value below $0=\Lambda_0(E)$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{rem:heuristic}
Let $(E_t)_{t\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a betting sequence with conditional \textsf{e}-power{} bounded below by
$c>0$, i.e.
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cond-epower}
   \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}\left[\log E_t\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}\right]\ \ge\ c
   \qquad\mathbb{P}_1\text{-a.s., for every }t\in\mathbb{N} .
\end{equation}
Then $\log W_t=\sum_{n\le t}\log E_n$ has $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[\log W_t]\ge tc\to\infty$,
which is the design principle behind Kelly betting \cite{Kel56,Bre61} and
growth-rate-optimal \textsf{e}-variables{} \cite{GHK24,LRR25}. The inference
``therefore $W_t$ exceeds $\frac1\alpha$ with high probability'' is what fails.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- construction-1: body_md -->
\label{con:nfl}
Let $c\in(0,\infty)$, $\alpha\in(0,1)$, $\eta\in(0,1)$ and $t\in\mathbb{N}$ be given,
and put $\ell:=\log\frac1\alpha$. Define constants
\begin{align}
   \tilde u&:=2c+1 , & M&:=(t-1)\tilde u+\ell , &
   u&:=\frac{c+(1-\eta)M}{\eta} ,
   \label{eq:nfl-constants}\\
   q&:=\frac{1-e^{-M}}{e^{u}-e^{-M}} , &
   \tilde q&:=\frac{1-e^{-1}}{e^{\tilde u}-e^{-1}} . & &
   \label{eq:nfl-probs}
\end{align}
Take $\mathcal{X}:=\{0,1\}$ with $\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{X}}:=2^{\mathcal{X}}$, $\Omega=\mathcal{X}^{\mathbb{N}}$, and let
$\mathbb{P}_0,\mathbb{P}_1$ be the laws on $(\Omega,\mathcal{B}_{\Omega})$ under which the
coordinates $X_1,X_2,\dots$ are independent with
\[
\begin{array}{lll}
   \mathbb{P}_1(X_1=1)=\eta , &\qquad
   \mathbb{P}_0(X_1=1)=q , &\\[2pt]
   \mathbb{P}_1(X_n=1)=\tfrac12 , &\qquad
   \mathbb{P}_0(X_n=1)=\tilde q , &\qquad n\ge2 .
\end{array}
\]
Define the betting sequence $E_n:\Omega\to(0,\infty)$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$, by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:nfl-bets}
   \log E_1:=\begin{cases} u, & X_1=1,\\ -M, & X_1=0,\end{cases}
   \qquad
   \log E_n:=\begin{cases} \tilde u, & X_n=1,\\ -1, & X_n=0,\end{cases}
   \quad n\ge2 .
\end{equation}
<!-- end construction-1 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:nfl-admissible}
$\tilde u>1>0$, $M\ge\ell>0$, $u>0$, and $q,\tilde q\in(0,1)$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
$\tilde u=2c+1>1$ since $c>0$; $M=(t-1)\tilde u+\ell\ge \ell>0$ since $t\ge1$;
$u=(c+(1-\eta)M)/\eta>0$ since $c>0$, $M>0$, $\eta\in(0,1)$. For $q$: the
numerator $1-e^{-M}$ lies in $(0,1)$ because $M>0$, and the denominator
satisfies $e^{u}-e^{-M}>1-e^{-M}>0$ because $u>0$; hence $q\in(0,1)$. The same
argument with $(\tilde u,1)$ in place of $(u,M)$ gives $\tilde q\in(0,1)$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:nfl-evar}
For every $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $E_n$ is $\mathcal{F}_n$-measurable and
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[E_n\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]=1$ $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Measurability is clear from \eqref{eq:nfl-bets}. Under $\mathbb{P}_0$ the
coordinates are independent, so $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[E_n\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]
=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[E_n]$. For $n=1$,
\[
   \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[E_1]=q\,e^{u}+(1-q)e^{-M} .
\]
Substituting $q$ from \eqref{eq:nfl-probs},
\[
   q\left( e^{u}-e^{-M}\right)+e^{-M}
   =\frac{1-e^{-M}}{e^{u}-e^{-M}}\left( e^{u}-e^{-M}\right)+e^{-M}
   =\left(1-e^{-M}\right)+e^{-M}=1 .
\]
For $n\ge2$ the identical computation with $(\tilde u,1,\tilde q)$ gives
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[E_n]=\tilde q e^{\tilde u}+(1-\tilde q)e^{-1}=1$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:nfl-epower}
For every $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[\log E_n\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]=c$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Again by independence the conditional expectation is the unconditional one. For
$n=1$, using $u=(c+(1-\eta)M)/\eta$ from \eqref{eq:nfl-constants},
\[
   \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[\log E_1]=\eta u-(1-\eta)M
   =\eta\cdot\frac{c+(1-\eta)M}{\eta}-(1-\eta)M=c .
\]
For $n\ge2$, using $\tilde u=2c+1$,
\[
   \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[\log E_n]=\tfrac12\tilde u-\tfrac12
   =\tfrac12(2c+1)-\tfrac12=c . \qedhere
\]
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:nfl-crash}
On the event $\{X_1=0\}$ one has $\max_{0\le n\le t}\log W_n\le \ell$, hence
$\tau_\alpha>t$.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Work on $\{X_1=0\}$. First, $\log W_0=0\le \ell$ since $\ell>0$. Second,
$\log W_1=\log E_1=-M<0\le \ell$. Third, for $2\le n\le t$, each of the increments
$\log E_2,\dots,\log E_n$ is at most $\tilde u$ by \eqref{eq:nfl-bets}, so
\[
   \log W_n=-M+\sum_{m=2}^{n}\log E_m\ \le\ -M+(n-1)\tilde u
   \ \le\ -M+(t-1)\tilde u\ =\ -\ell\ \le\ \ell ,
\]
the last two steps by $n\le t$ and by $M=(t-1)\tilde u+\ell$ from
\eqref{eq:nfl-constants}. Hence $\max_{0\le n\le t}\log W_n\le \ell$, i.e.\
$W_n\le\frac1\alpha$ for all $n\le t$, i.e.\ $\tau_\alpha>t$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:nfl}
Let $c\in(0,\infty)$, $\alpha\in(0,1)$, $\eta\in(0,1)$ and $t\in\mathbb{N}$. The pair
$(\mathbb{P}_0,\mathbb{P}_1)$ and the betting sequence of \Cref{con:nfl} --- both of which
depend on $(c,\alpha,\eta,t)$ --- satisfy
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.4em]
\item $E_n$ is a conditional \textsf{e}-variable{} for $\mathbb{P}_0$ at time $n$, with
      $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[E_n\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]=1$, for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$;
\item $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[\log E_n\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]=c$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.\ for every
      $n\in\mathbb{N}$;
\item $\bar\gamma_t(\alpha)\ \ge\ 1-\eta$, and therefore also
      $\gamma_t(\alpha)\ge1-\eta$.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently there is no function $\Phi:(0,\infty)\times(0,1)\times\mathbb{N}\to[0,1)$
such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:nophi}
   \bar\gamma_t(\alpha)\ \le\ \Phi(c,\alpha,t)
   \qquad\text{for every pair of hypotheses and every betting sequence
   satisfying \eqref{eq:cond-epower}:}
\end{equation}
no bound on the type-II error is a function of the \textsf{e}-power{} level $c$, the
significance level $\alpha$ and the horizon $t$ alone, \emph{uniformly over
testing problems}.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{rem:quantifier}
The pair $(\mathbb{P}_0,\mathbb{P}_1)$ of \Cref{con:nfl} is built from
$(c,\alpha,\eta,t)$: the alternative puts mass $\eta$ on $\{X_1=1\}$, and the
null probability $q$ of \eqref{eq:nfl-probs} depends on $\eta$ through $u$. Driving $\eta$ to $0$ against a candidate $\Phi$ therefore varies the
testing problem as well as the design, and \eqref{eq:nophi} is a statement about
the class of \emph{all} testing problems.

This is the right quantifier for a sample-size rule, which must be written down
before the data and cannot depend on the unknown alternative. It is not the
strongest conceivable statement, and the stronger one is false: a
\emph{model-dependent} bound $\Phi(c,\alpha,t;P_0,P_1)$ is not excluded by
\Cref{thm:nfl}, and in some models it exists. Work in the i.i.d.\ model
(\Cref{def:iid}) and suppose $R\le R_{\max}$ $P_0$-a.s.\ and $c>\ell$. Since $\mathcal{F}_0$ is trivial, $E_1\in\mathcal{E}$, and with
$A:=\{E_1>\frac1\alpha\}$ and $\pi:=P_1(A)$ we have $\log E_1\le\ell$ on
$A^{c}$, while Jensen and $\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[E_1]=\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[RE_1]\le R_{\max}$ give
$\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[\log E_1\mathbf 1_A]\le\pi\log(R_{\max}/\pi)$. Hence
\[
   c\ \le\ \pi\log\frac{R_{\max}}{\pi}+(1-\pi)\ell ,
\]
whose right-hand side tends to $\ell$ as $\pi\downarrow0$; so $c>\ell$ forces
$\pi\ge\pi_0(c,\alpha,R_{\max})>0$, and since
$\{\tau_\alpha>t\}\subseteq\{\tau_\alpha>1\}$,
\[
   \bar\gamma_t(\alpha)\ \le\ \bar\gamma_1(\alpha)=1-\pi\ \le\ 1-\pi_0\ <\ 1
   \qquad\text{for every }t .
\]
The class is nonempty whenever $c\le\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)$ (take $E_n=R(X_n)$), so the
two conditions $\ell<c\le\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)$ are jointly satisfiable --- for instance
$P_0=\mathrm{Bern}(10^{-3})$, $P_1=\mathrm{Bern}(0.9)$, $\alpha=0.05$, where
$R_{\max}=900$, $\ell=2.996$ and $\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)=5.892$. The regime is a
degenerate one --- it requires the \textsf{e}-power{} of a single observation to exceed
$\log\frac1\alpha$, i.e.\ one expects to reject before seeing two data points ---
but it shows that \Cref{thm:nfl} is a statement about uniformity over models and
not only over designs.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
(i) is \Cref{lem:nfl-evar}, (ii) is \Cref{lem:nfl-epower}. For (iii),
\Cref{lem:nfl-crash} gives $\{X_1=0\}\subseteq\{\tau_\alpha>t\}$, and
$\mathbb{P}_1(X_1=0)=1-\eta$ by construction; \Cref{lem:order} gives the second
inequality. For the final claim, suppose such a $\Phi$ existed and fix
$c,\alpha,t$. Choosing $\eta:=\frac12\left(1-\Phi(c,\alpha,t)\right)\in(0,1)$ yields a
sequence with conditional \textsf{e}-power{} exactly $c$ and
$\bar\gamma_t(\alpha)\ge1-\eta=\frac12\left(1+\Phi(c,\alpha,t)\right)>\Phi(c,\alpha,t)$,
a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:nfl}
Take $c=0.1$, $\alpha=0.05$, $\eta=\frac12$, $t=10$. Then
$\ell=\log20=2.995732$, and \eqref{eq:nfl-constants}--\eqref{eq:nfl-probs} give
\[
   \tilde u=1.2,\qquad
   M=9\cdot1.2+2.995732=13.795732,\qquad
   u=\frac{0.1+0.5\cdot13.795732}{0.5}=13.995732 ,
\]
\[
   q=\frac{1-e^{-13.795732}}{e^{13.995732}-e^{-13.795732}}=8.350842\cdot10^{-7},
   \qquad
   \tilde q=\frac{1-e^{-1}}{e^{1.2}-e^{-1}}=0.2141158 .
\]
In words: at the first step the bet pays $e^{13.996}\approx1.2\cdot10^{6}$ on an
event of null probability $8.4\cdot10^{-7}$ and alternative probability
$\frac12$, and otherwise loses all but $e^{-13.796}\approx10^{-6}$ of the
wealth. Every step has \textsf{e}-power{} exactly $0.1$. The four requirements read
\[
   \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[E_1]=1,\quad \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[E_n]=1,\quad
   \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[\log E_n]=0.1,\quad
   -M+(t-1)\tilde u=-2.995732=-\ell ,
\]
and enumeration of all $2^{10}$ paths gives
\[
   \bar\gamma_{10}(0.05)\ =\ 0.500000\ =\ 1-\eta
\]
exactly: on $\{X_1=1\}$ the test rejects already at $t=1$, and on $\{X_1=0\}$ it
never rejects by $t=10$. So a test whose \textsf{e}-power{} promises
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[\log W_{10}]=1.0$ nats of evidence has power exactly $\frac12$ at
this horizon --- and by \Cref{thm:nfl} the same construction drives the power to
$0$ for any fixed $c$, $\alpha$ and $t$.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prp:powerone}
Work in the i.i.d.\ model. Let $E\in\mathcal{E}$ with $\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[\log E]>0$, and let
$(W_t)_{t\in\mathbb{N}_0}$
be the i.i.d.\ product generated by $E$. Then $\tau_\alpha<\infty$
$\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.\ for every $\alpha\in(0,1)$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
By \Cref{lem:epower-welldef} $\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[(\log E)_+]<\infty$, so
$\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[\log E]>0$ already forces $\log E\in L^{1}(P_1)$. By the strong law of
large numbers, $t^{-1}\log W_t\to\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[\log E]>0$
$\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s., so $\log W_t\to+\infty$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s., and in particular
$\log W_t>\ell$ for some $t$.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{rem:alone}
\Cref{thm:nfl} is a statement about a \emph{class}: the class of betting
sequences whose conditional \textsf{e}-power{} is at least $c$ admits no type-II bound
depending only on $(c,\alpha,t)$. It is not the statement that \textsf{e}-power{}
carries no information. A positive \textsf{e}-power{} does control the asymptotics
(\Cref{prp:powerone}: the test rejects eventually, almost surely), and it does
control the \emph{mean} of $\log W_t$ by construction. The two results are not
in conflict, and the difference between them is the difference between a
pointwise limit and a uniform bound: \Cref{prp:powerone} fixes one \textsf{e}-variable{} and
lets $t\to\infty$, while \Cref{thm:nfl} fixes $t$ and varies the sequence, which
it is free to do because the crash depth $M=(t-1)\tilde u+\ell$ may depend on
$t$. What fails is not consistency but \emph{uniformity over the class defined
by \textsf{e}-power{} alone} --- and uniformity is what a sample-size calculation
requires. The missing ingredient is any control of the lower tail, and
\Cref{rem:whatworks} and \Cref{sec:ceiling} supply it. Note finally that the
hypothesis of \Cref{thm:nfl} is the favourable one, \textsf{e}-power{} bounded
\emph{below} by a positive constant: were it negative there would be nothing to
discuss, not even \Cref{prp:powerone}, so the theorem is not an artefact of a
degenerate case.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
\label{rem:whatworks}
Inspection of \Cref{con:nfl} shows the free parameter is the depth $M$ of the
crash, which \eqref{eq:cond-epower} does not constrain. Any hypothesis bounding
the lower tail of $\log E_t$ restores a bound. Suppose, for some
$s_0>0$ and $c_0>0$,
\[
   \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}\left[ E_t^{-s_0}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}\right]\ \le\ e^{-c_0}
   \qquad\mathbb{P}_1\text{-a.s., for every }t\in\mathbb{N} .
\]
The tower-property induction of \Cref{prp:upper-seq}\ref{it:agg-exact}, run with $\le$ in
place of $\ge$, gives $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[W_t^{-s_0}]\le e^{-tc_0}$, i.e.\
$\Lambda^{(t)}_{s_0}\ge c_0$, and \Cref{lem:chernoff} then gives
$\gamma_t(\alpha)\le\exp(s_0\ell-tc_0)\to0$. The exponent $\Lambda^{(t)}$ of
\Cref{def:exponent} is the sharpest such summary, and \Cref{sec:ceiling}
determines exactly how large it can be.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
\label{rem:cramer}
For an i.i.d.\ product the exponential case is settled exactly, and in both
directions, by \Cref{prp:exponent}: under its hypotheses
$\lim_{t}-\frac1t\log\gamma_t(\alpha)=\Lambda(E)$, so the fixed-horizon error decays
exponentially if and only if $\Lambda(E)>0$, i.e.\ if and only if
$\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[E^{-s}]<1$ for some $s>0$. Given positive \textsf{e}-power{} this is in turn
equivalent to \emph{Cram\'er's moment condition},
$\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[E^{-s_0}]<\infty$ for some
$s_0>0$: that condition makes $\varphi(s):=\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[E^{-s}]$ finite on
$[0,s_0]$, by Lyapunov's inequality $\varphi(s)\le\varphi(s_0)^{s/s_0}$, with
$\varphi(0)=1$; and the difference quotients
$\frac{\varphi(s)-1}{s}=\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[\frac{e^{-s\log E}-1}{s}]$ decrease as
$s\downarrow0$ and are dominated above by their value at $s_0$, so monotone
convergence gives the right derivative
$\varphi'(0^{+})=-\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[\log E]<0$, and $\varphi(s)<1$ for small $s>0$. It is a hypothesis on the lower tail: by Markov's inequality it
gives $\mathbb{P}_1(E\le\epsilon)\le\epsilon^{s_0}\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[E^{-s_0}]$, a
polynomially small crash probability, and conversely
$\mathbb{P}_1(E\le\epsilon)\le K\epsilon^{a}$ gives finiteness for every $s<a$. The
likelihood ratio satisfies it for free with $s_0=1$, since
$\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[R^{-1}]=P_0(R>0)\le1$; it constrains the \emph{approximation} to $R$
that one bets with, not the testing problem.

What Cram\'er's condition is not is necessary for a bound. If
$\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[\log E]=:m>0$ and $\sigma^{2}:=\operatorname{Var}_{P_1}(\log E)<\infty$ --- which
permits a lower tail with no exponential moment whatsoever --- then Chebyshev's
inequality applied to $\log W_t$ gives, for every $t>\ell/m$,
\[
   \gamma_t(\alpha)\ \le\ \frac{t\,\sigma^{2}}{\left( t\,m-\ell\right)^{2}}
   \ =\ \frac{\sigma^{2}}{m^{2}\,t}\,(1+o(1)) ,
\]
a bound of order $1/t$ which holds \emph{even in the regime where Cram\'er's
moment condition fails and $\Lambda(E)=0$}. So \Cref{thm:nfl} separates
\emph{no} hypothesis on the lower tail from \emph{some} hypothesis, while
Cram\'er's moment condition separates exponential from sub-exponential decay;
under the additional hypothesis $\sigma^{2}<\infty$ the sub-exponential rate is
$O(1/t)$. The two dichotomies are different, and only the second is an
equivalence.

Which \emph{quantitative} bound each hypothesis buys is the subject of the
companion paper \cite{LADDER}: Cram\'er's condition, a crash tail with one of
three further moment conditions, a conditional variance with a wealth floor, a
sub-Gaussian or bounded-tilt lower tail, a bounded log-increment, and i.i.d.\
increments form a partial order of hypotheses, each supplying a majorant for
the conditional cumulant generating function of $\log E_n$ and hence, by one
Legendre transform, an explicit exponent. That paper works with an arbitrary
filtration, asks only that the certified drift and the majorant be predictable,
and needs neither a product structure nor the results proved here; conversely
nothing below uses it.
The two papers meet at exactly one point, its top rung: there the majorant may
be taken to be the truth, the exponent is $\Lambda(E)$, and \Cref{sec:ceiling}
is what bounds $\Lambda(E)$ itself.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
\label{def:Zbeta}
In the i.i.d.\ model define
\[
   Z:\mathbb{R}\to(0,\infty],\qquad Z_\beta:=\mathbb{E}_{P_0}\left[ R^{\beta}\right] ,
\]
and
\[
   \lambda:\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}\to[-\infty,\infty],\qquad
   \lambda(\beta):=-\frac1\beta\log Z_\beta .
\]
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
\label{def:flattened}
In the i.i.d.\ model put
\[
   \mathcal{B}\ :=\ \left\{\beta>0\;\middle|\; Z_\beta<\infty\right\} ,
   \qquad
   \beta_{\max}\ :=\ \sup\mathcal{B}\ \in[1,\infty] ,
\]
so that $\mathcal{B}$ is an interval with $(0,1]\subseteq\mathcal{B}\subseteq(0,\beta_{\max}]$ ---
the first inclusion because $Z_\beta\le1$ on $(0,1]$ by \Cref{lem:Zf}(i) --- and
for $\beta\in\mathcal{B}$ define
\[
   R_\beta:\mathcal{X}\to[0,\infty),\qquad R_\beta:=\frac{R^{\beta}}{Z_\beta} ,
\]
so that $R_1=R$ and $\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[R_\beta]=1$, whence $R_\beta\in\mathcal{E}$ for every
$\beta\in\mathcal{B}$.
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- definition-13: body_md -->
\label{def:renyi}
Let $Q,P$ be probability measures on $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{X}})$, let $\mu$ be any
$\sigma$-finite measure with $Q,P\ll\mu$, and put $q:=\frac{dQ}{d\mu}$,
$p:=\frac{dP}{d\mu}$. For $a\in(0,1)$ define
\[
   \mathrm{D}_a(Q\|P):=\frac{1}{a-1}\log\int q^{a}p^{1-a}\,d\mu\ \in[0,\infty] .
\]
The value does not depend on the choice of $\mu$, and no absolute continuity
between $Q$ and $P$ is required; when $Q\ll P$ it reduces to
$\frac{1}{a-1}\log\mathbb{E}_{P}[(\frac{dQ}{dP})^{a}]$.
<!-- end definition-13 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
\label{rem:renyigenerality}
\Cref{ass:standing} assumes $P_1\ll P_0$ but not the converse, so
$\frac{dP_0}{dP_1}$ need not exist; the identity
$\lambda(\beta)=\mathrm{D}_{1-\beta}(P_0\|P_1)$ of \Cref{lem:Zf}(iii) would be
meaningless under a definition requiring $P_0\ll P_1$. The model
$P_0=\mathrm{Bern}(\frac12)$, $P_1=\delta_1$ of \Cref{rem:eqcase} satisfies
\Cref{ass:standing} and has $P_0\not\ll P_1$.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:Zf}
Under \Cref{ass:standing}, in the i.i.d.\ model:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.4em]
\item $Z_\beta\in(0,1]$ for every $\beta\in(0,1]$ --- so on that range $Z$ and
      $\lambda$ take the values announced in \Cref{def:Zbeta} --- and $Z_1=1$, so
      $\lambda(1)=0$ and $\lambda(\beta)\in[0,\infty)$ for every
      $\beta\in(0,1]$ --- only $\lim_{\beta\downarrow0}\lambda(\beta)$ can be
      infinite;
\item $\lambda$ is nonincreasing on $(0,1]$;
\item for $\beta\in(0,1)$, $\lambda(\beta)=\mathrm{D}_{1-\beta}(P_0\|P_1)$, the
      R\'enyi divergence of \Cref{def:renyi} of order $1-\beta$ (skew symmetry,
      \cite[Prop.~2]{vEH14}; see \Cref{thm:app-renyi});
\item if moreover $\log R$ is not $P_0$-a.s.\ constant, then $\lambda$ is strictly
      decreasing on $(0,1]$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
(i) $Z_1=\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[R]=1$. For $\beta\in(0,1)$ the map $x\mapsto x^{\beta}$ is
concave on $[0,\infty)$, so Jensen gives
$Z_\beta=\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[R^{\beta}]\le(\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[R])^{\beta}=1$; and $Z_\beta>0$ because
$P_0(R>0)>0$. Hence $\log Z_\beta\le0$ and $\lambda(\beta)\ge0$.

(ii) Let $0<\beta'\le\beta\le1$ and put $\rho:=\beta'/\beta\in(0,1]$. Applying
Jensen to the concave map $x\mapsto x^{\rho}$,
\[
   Z_{\beta'}=\mathbb{E}_{P_0}\left[\left( R^{\beta}\right)^{\rho}\right]
   \ \le\ \left(\mathbb{E}_{P_0}\left[ R^{\beta}\right]\right)^{\rho}=Z_\beta^{\rho} ,
\]
so $\log Z_{\beta'}\le\rho\log Z_\beta$ and, dividing by $-\beta'=-\rho\beta<0$,
$\lambda(\beta')\ge \lambda(\beta)$.

(iii) With $\mu$, $p_0$, $p_1$ as in \Cref{def:renyi} and $\beta\in(0,1)$,
\[
   \int p_0^{1-\beta}p_1^{\beta}\,d\mu
   =\int_{\{p_0>0\}}p_0\,R^{\beta}\,d\mu=Z_\beta ,
\]
the integrand vanishing where $p_0=0$ because $1-\beta>0$; hence
$\mathrm{D}_{1-\beta}(P_0\|P_1)=\frac{1}{-\beta}\log Z_\beta=\lambda(\beta)$. No
absolute continuity of $P_0$ with respect to $P_1$ is used. (This is the skew-symmetry identity
$\mathrm{D}_a(P\|Q)=\frac{a}{1-a}\mathrm{D}_{1-a}(Q\|P)$ of \cite[Prop.~2]{vEH14}, written
out.)

(iv) This is (ii) with strict Jensen. Let $0<\beta'<\beta\le1$, so
$\rho=\beta'/\beta\in(0,1)$ and $x\mapsto x^{\rho}$ is \emph{strictly} concave
on $[0,\infty)$. The variable $R^{\beta}$ is $P_0$-integrable
($\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[R^{\beta}]=Z_\beta\le1$) and is not $P_0$-a.s.\ constant, because
$\log R$ is not; hence Jensen's inequality is strict,
$Z_{\beta'}<Z_\beta^{\rho}$. Taking $\log$ and dividing by $-\beta'=-\rho\beta<0$
gives $\lambda(\beta')>\lambda(\beta)$.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- definition-14: body_md -->
\label{def:condZ}
For $t\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\beta\in(0,1]$ define the $\mathcal{F}_{t-1}$-measurable variables
\[
   Z_{\beta,t}:=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}\left[ R_t^{\beta}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}\right] ,
   \qquad
   \lambda_t(\beta):=-\frac1\beta\log Z_{\beta,t} ,
\]
with $R_t$ as in \Cref{def:ratios}. In the i.i.d.\ model
$Z_{\beta,t}=Z_\beta$ and $\lambda_t(\beta)=\lambda(\beta)$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.\ for
every $t$; in particular both are $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.\ equal to constants.
<!-- end definition-14 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:Zf-cond}
Under \Cref{ass:standing}, for every $t\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s.\ --- hence also
$\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.4em]
\item $Z_{\beta,t}\in(0,1]$ for every $\beta\in(0,1]$, and $Z_{1,t}=1$; hence
      $\lambda_t(1)=0$ and $\lambda_t(\beta)\in[0,\infty)$ for every
      $\beta\in(0,1]$;
\item $\beta\mapsto\lambda_t(\beta)$ is nonincreasing on $(0,1]$, so that
      \[
         \lambda_t(0^{+}):=\lim_{\beta\downarrow0}\lambda_t(\beta)
         \ =\ \sup_{\beta\in(0,1]}\lambda_t(\beta)\ \in[0,\infty]
      \]
      exists.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Each $Z_{\beta,t}$ is a conditional expectation, hence defined up to a null set
for each fixed $\beta$ separately. Fix versions for $\beta\in(0,1]\cap\mathbb{Q}$ and
read (i) and (ii) as holding, off one null set, simultaneously for rational
$\beta$; this is all that is used, since \Cref{cor:ceiling} fixes a single
$\beta$ and $\lambda_t(0^{+})$ may be defined as the supremum over rational
$\beta$, which by (ii) is the same limit.

(i) $Z_{1,t}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[R_t\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]=1$ $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s.: on
$\left\{ L_{t-1}>0\right\}$ this is the $\mathbb{P}_0$-martingale property of $L$, and on
$\left\{ L_{t-1}=0\right\}$ it is the convention $R_t:=1$ of \Cref{def:ratios}. For
$\beta\in(0,1)$ the map $x\mapsto x^{\beta}$ is concave on $[0,\infty)$, so
conditional Jensen gives $Z_{\beta,t}\le(\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[R_t\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}])^{\beta}=1$
$\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s.; and $Z_{\beta,t}>0$ $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s., since $Z_{\beta,t}=0$ on an
$\mathcal{F}_{t-1}$-set of positive $\mathbb{P}_0$-measure would force $R_t=0$ $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s.\
there, contradicting $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[R_t\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]=1$. Therefore
$\log Z_{\beta,t}\le0$ and $\lambda_t(\beta)\ge0$.

(ii) Let $0<\beta'\le\beta\le1$ and $\rho:=\beta'/\beta\in(0,1]$. Conditional
Jensen for the concave $x\mapsto x^{\rho}$ gives
$Z_{\beta',t}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[(R_t^{\beta})^{\rho}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]
\le Z_{\beta,t}^{\rho}$, so $\log Z_{\beta',t}\le\rho\log Z_{\beta,t}$ and,
dividing by $-\beta'=-\rho\beta<0$, $\lambda_t(\beta')\ge\lambda_t(\beta)$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
\label{rem:Zf-cond}
By \Cref{lem:Zf-cond}(i), $\left\{0<Z_{\beta,t}<\infty\right\}$ has full $\mathbb{P}_0$-measure,
so conventions off it are harmless under either measure. And
$\beta\mapsto\log Z_{\beta,t}$ is a conditional cumulant generating function of
$\log R_t$ under $\mathbb{P}_0$, hence convex on $\mathbb{R}$, with the value $0$ at
$\beta=1$; it also takes the value $0$ at $\beta=0$ whenever
$\mathbb{P}_0(R_t>0\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1})=1$.
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:upper-cond}
Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a betting sequence, let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $s\in(0,\infty)$,
and set $\beta:=\frac{1}{1+s}\in(0,1)$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:upper-cond}
   \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}\left[ E_n^{-s}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}\right]\ \ge\ e^{-\lambda_n(\beta)}
   \qquad\mathbb{P}_1\text{-a.s.}
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
\emph{Step 1 (factorisation).} On $\left\{0<E_n<\infty\right\}$, using
$1-\beta-s\beta=1-\beta-(1-\beta)=0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:factor-cond}
   E_n^{\,1-\beta}\left( R_nE_n^{-s}\right)^{\beta}
   \ =\ R_n^{\beta}\,E_n^{\,1-\beta-s\beta}
   \ =\ R_n^{\beta} .
\end{equation}
We dispose of the degenerate cases. By \Cref{lem:supmg} $E_n<\infty$
$\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s., hence $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.\ by \Cref{ass:standing}. And on
$\left\{ E_n=0\right\}$ we have $E_n^{-s}=+\infty$, so on the event
$\left\{\mathbb{P}_1(E_n=0\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1})>0\right\}$ the left-hand side of
\eqref{eq:upper-cond} is $+\infty$ and there is nothing to prove; on the
complement $\mathbb{P}_1(E_n=0\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1})=0$. That is a $\mathbb{P}_1$-statement and
the conditional expectation below is taken under $\mathbb{P}_0$, so the two must be
linked: by \Cref{lem:bayes},
$\mathbb{P}_1(E_n=0\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[R_n\mathbf 1_{\{E_n=0\}}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]$,
so on that complement $R_n\mathbf 1_{\{E_n=0\}}=0$ \emph{$\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s.} Hence
$\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s.\ there either $E_n>0$, where \eqref{eq:factor-cond} is the
displayed algebra, or $R_n=0$, where both of its sides vanish (using
$\beta>0$). So \eqref{eq:factor-cond} may be used inside
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[\,\cdot\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]$.

\emph{Step 2 (conditional H\"older).} The exponents $\frac1{1-\beta}$ and
$\frac1\beta$ are conjugate. Conditional H\"older (\Cref{cor:app-holder}) under
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[\,\cdot\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]$, applied to \eqref{eq:factor-cond}, gives, $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.,
\[
   Z_{\beta,n}
   =\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}\left[ E_n^{\,1-\beta}\left( R_nE_n^{-s}\right)^{\beta}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}\right]
   \ \le\ \left(\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}\left[ E_n\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}\right]\right)^{1-\beta}
          \left(\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}\left[ R_nE_n^{-s}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}\right]\right)^{\beta} .
\]

\emph{Step 3 (the two conditional constraints).} The first factor is at most
$1$, by \Cref{def:cond-evar} and $1-\beta>0$. The second is
$(\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[E_n^{-s}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}])^{\beta}$, by \Cref{lem:bayes} applied to
$Y=E_n^{-s}$. Hence
$Z_{\beta,n}\le(\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[E_n^{-s}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}])^{\beta}$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.

\emph{Step 4 (rearranging).} Both sides are positive $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.\ by
\Cref{lem:Zf-cond}(i); taking $\log$ and multiplying by $-\frac1\beta<0$
reverses the inequality and gives
$\lambda_n(\beta)\ge-\log\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[E_n^{-s}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]$, which is
\eqref{eq:upper-cond}.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:upper}
Let $E\in\mathcal{E}$ and $s\in(0,\infty)$, and set
\[
   \beta:=\frac{1}{1+s}\in(0,1),\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
   s=\frac{1-\beta}{\beta} .
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:upper}
   \Lambda_s(E)\ \le\ \lambda(\beta) ,
\end{equation}
with equality if and only if $E=R^{\beta}/Z_\beta$ $P_0$-a.s.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Fix a $\sigma$-finite measure $\mu$ dominating $P_0$ (for instance $\mu=P_0$)
and write $p_0:=\frac{dP_0}{d\mu}$, $p_1:=\frac{dP_1}{d\mu}$, so that
$R=p_1/p_0$ on $\{p_0>0\}$ and $Z_\beta=\int p_0^{1-\beta}p_1^{\beta}\,d\mu$.

\emph{Step 1 (factorisation).} On $\{0<E<\infty\}$ we have, using
$1-\beta-s\beta=1-\beta-(1-\beta)=0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:factor}
   \left( p_0E\right)^{1-\beta}\left( p_1E^{-s}\right)^{\beta}
   \ =\ p_0^{1-\beta}p_1^{\beta}\,E^{\,1-\beta-s\beta}
   \ =\ p_0^{1-\beta}p_1^{\beta} .
\end{equation}
We dispose of two degenerate cases first. If $P_1(E=0)>0$ then
$\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[E^{-s}]=\infty$, so $\Lambda_s(E)=-\infty$ and \eqref{eq:upper} is
trivial; \emph{assume henceforth $P_1(E=0)=0$}. And $P_0(E=\infty)>0$ would give
$\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[E]=\infty>1$, contradicting $E\in\mathcal{E}$, so $P_0(E=\infty)=0$.
Consequently $p_1=0$ $\mu$-a.e.\ on $\{E=0\}$ and $p_0=0$ $\mu$-a.e.\ on
$\{E=\infty\}$, and on both of those sets the two sides of \eqref{eq:factor}
vanish (using $1-\beta>0$ and $\beta>0$). Hence \eqref{eq:factor} holds
$\mu$-a.e.\ on $\mathcal{X}$.

\emph{Step 2 (H\"older).} The exponents $\frac{1}{1-\beta}$ and $\frac1\beta$
are conjugate, since $(1-\beta)+\beta=1$. Applying H\"older's inequality
\cite[Thm.~3.5]{Rud87} (\Cref{thm:app-holder}) to \eqref{eq:factor},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:holderstep}
\begin{split}
   Z_\beta&=\int\left( p_0E\right)^{1-\beta}\left( p_1E^{-s}\right)^{\beta}d\mu
   \ \le\ \left(\int p_0E\,d\mu\right)^{1-\beta}
          \left(\int p_1E^{-s}\,d\mu\right)^{\beta}\\[2pt]
   &=\left(\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[E]\right)^{1-\beta}\left(\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[E^{-s}]\right)^{\beta} .
\end{split}
\end{equation}

\emph{Step 3 (using the constraint).} $\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[E]\le1$ and $1-\beta>0$, so
$(\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[E])^{1-\beta}\le1$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:afterconstraint}
   Z_\beta\ \le\ \left(\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[E^{-s}]\right)^{\beta} .
\end{equation}

\emph{Step 4 (rearranging).} Both sides of \eqref{eq:afterconstraint} are
positive; taking $\log$ and multiplying by $-\frac1\beta<0$ reverses the
inequality:
\[
   \lambda(\beta)=-\frac1\beta\log Z_\beta
   \ \ge\ -\log\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[E^{-s}]=\Lambda_s(E) ,
\]
which is \eqref{eq:upper}.

\emph{Step 5 (equality).} Equality in \eqref{eq:holderstep} holds if and only
if $p_0E$ and $p_1E^{-s}$ are proportional $\mu$-a.e., say
$c_1\,p_0E=c_2\,p_1E^{-s}$ with $c_1,c_2\ge0$ not both zero. We use this on all
of $\mathcal{X}$, not only where $p_1>0$. On $\{p_0>0,\,p_1>0\}$ we have
$E\in(0,\infty)$ $\mu$-a.e.\ (Step 1), so $c_1,c_2>0$ there and
$E^{1+s}=\frac{c_2}{c_1}\,\frac{p_1}{p_0}=\frac{c_2}{c_1}R$, i.e.\
$E=\varkappa R^{\beta}$ with $\varkappa:=(c_2/c_1)^{\beta}$, using
$\frac{1}{1+s}=\beta$. On $\{p_0>0,\,p_1=0\}$ the right-hand side vanishes, so
$p_0E=0$ and hence $E=0=R^{\beta}$ there. Therefore
\[
   E\ =\ \varkappa\,R^{\beta}\qquad P_0\text{-a.s.\ on all of }\mathcal{X} ,
\]
and only now does the constraint enter: equality in Step 3 requires
$\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[E]=1$, which reads $\varkappa Z_\beta=1$, i.e.\
$\varkappa=Z_\beta^{-1}$. Conversely $E=R^{\beta}/Z_\beta$ gives equality
throughout.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prp:upper-seq}
Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be any betting sequence, with wealth process
$(W_t)_{t\in\mathbb{N}_0}$, and let $s\in(0,\infty)$, $\beta=\frac1{1+s}$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),leftmargin=2.4em]
\item\label{it:agg-exact} for every $t\in\mathbb{N}$,
      \begin{equation}\label{eq:upper-seq-exact}
         \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}\left[ W_t^{-s}\exp\left(\sum_{n\le t}\lambda_n(\beta)\right)\right]
         \ \ge\ 1 ;
      \end{equation}
\item\label{it:agg-det} if $\bar\lambda_n(\beta)\in[0,\infty]$ are constants
      with $\lambda_n(\beta)\le\bar\lambda_n(\beta)$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s., then
      \begin{equation}\label{eq:upper-seq-det}
         \Lambda^{(t)}_s\ \le\ \frac1t\sum_{n\le t}\bar\lambda_n(\beta)
         \qquad\text{for every }t\in\mathbb{N} ;
      \end{equation}
\item\label{it:agg-iid} in the i.i.d.\ model, $\Lambda^{(t)}_s\le\lambda(\beta)$
      for every $t\in\mathbb{N}$, with equality for a given $t$ if and only if
      $E_n=R_\beta(X_n)$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.\ for every $n\le t$, with $R_\beta$ as in
      \Cref{def:flattened} --- equivalently $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s., when $P_0\sim P_1$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
\emph{\ref{it:agg-exact}.} Put
$M_t:=W_t^{-s}\exp(\sum_{n\le t}\lambda_n(\beta))$, so $M_0=1$. By
\Cref{lem:supmg} and \Cref{ass:standing}, $E_n<\infty$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s., so
$W_n^{-s}=W_{n-1}^{-s}E_n^{-s}$ holds $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.\ (the identity can fail
only where some $E_n=\infty$). Each $\lambda_k(\beta)$ with $k\le n$ is
$\mathcal{F}_{n-1}$-measurable, and $W_{n-1}^{-s}$ is nonnegative and
$\mathcal{F}_{n-1}$-measurable, so the pull-out property and \Cref{thm:upper-cond} give
\[
   \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}\left[ M_n\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}\right]
   \ =\ M_{n-1}\,e^{\lambda_n(\beta)}\,
        \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}\left[ E_n^{-s}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}\right]
   \ \ge\ M_{n-1}
   \qquad\mathbb{P}_1\text{-a.s.}
\]
Taking expectations and inducting from $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[M_0]=1$ gives
\eqref{eq:upper-seq-exact}.

\emph{\ref{it:agg-det}.} From $\lambda_n(\beta)\le\bar\lambda_n(\beta)$ we get
$M_t\le W_t^{-s}\exp(\sum_{n\le t}\bar\lambda_n(\beta))$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s., so
\eqref{eq:upper-seq-exact} gives
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[W_t^{-s}]\ge\exp(-\sum_{n\le t}\bar\lambda_n(\beta))$; take
$-\frac1t\log$.

\emph{\ref{it:agg-iid}.} In the i.i.d.\ model $\lambda_n(\beta)=\lambda(\beta)$
$\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.\ for every $n$, so \ref{it:agg-det} applies with
$\bar\lambda_n(\beta)=\lambda(\beta)$ and yields
$\Lambda^{(t)}_s\le\lambda(\beta)$. For the equality case, note first that
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[E_n^{-s}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]\ge e^{-\lambda(\beta)}$ is
\Cref{thm:upper-cond}, and that by \Cref{lem:flat}
$\Lambda_s(R_\beta)=\lambda(\beta)$; so if $E_n=R_\beta(X_n)$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.\ for
all $n\le t$ then every inequality in the induction above is an equality and
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[W_t^{-s}]=e^{-t\lambda(\beta)}$. Conversely suppose
$\Lambda^{(t)}_s=\lambda(\beta)$, i.e.\
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[W_t^{-s}]=e^{-t\lambda(\beta)}\in(0,\infty)$. Running the
induction from index $n$ to index $t$ gives
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[W_n^{-s}]\le e^{(t-n)\lambda(\beta)}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[W_t^{-s}]<\infty$
for every $n\le t$, so every term in the chain is finite and positive and each
inequality must be an equality. Since $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[E_n\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]\le1$
forces $E_n<\infty$ $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s., and $\mathbb{P}_1\ll\mathbb{P}_0$ on $\mathcal{F}_t$, we have
$W_{n-1}^{-s}>0$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.; hence equality at the $n$-th step forces
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[E_n^{-s}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]=e^{-\lambda(\beta)}$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s. Now
write $E_n=g_n(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ with $g_n$ measurable and, for
$y\in\mathcal{X}^{n-1}$, put $E_n^{y}(x):=g_n(y,x)$. Because $\mathbb{P}_i=P_i^{\otimes\mathbb{N}}$,
Fubini's theorem gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fubini}
   \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_i}\left[ h(E_n)\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}\right]
   =\mathbb{E}_{P_i}\left[ h\left( E_n^{Y}\right)\right]\Big|_{Y=(X_1,\dots,X_{n-1})}
   \qquad\mathbb{P}_i\text{-a.s.}
\end{equation}
for every measurable $h:[0,\infty]\to[0,\infty]$. With $i=0$ and
$h=\mathrm{id}$ this says $E_n^{y}\in\mathcal{E}$ for $P_0^{\otimes(n-1)}$-a.e.\ $y$,
hence for $P_1^{\otimes(n-1)}$-a.e.\ $y$ since $P_1\ll P_0$; with $i=1$ and
$h(x)=x^{-s}$ it turns the displayed equality into
$\Lambda_s(E_n^{y})=\lambda(\beta)$ for $P_1^{\otimes(n-1)}$-a.e.\ $y$. The
equality case of \Cref{thm:upper} identifies $E_n^{y}=R_\beta$ $P_0$-a.s., hence
also $P_1$-a.s.; that is, $E_n=R_\beta(X_n)$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- remark-12: body_md -->
\label{rem:eqcase}
Under \Cref{ass:standing} alone the conclusion of \Cref{prp:upper-seq} cannot be
strengthened to $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s. Take $\mathcal{X}=\{0,1\}$,
$P_0=\mathrm{Bern}(\frac12)$ and $P_1=\delta_1$, so that $P_1\ll P_0$ and
$\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)=\log2<\infty$; here $R=2\cdot\mathbf 1_{\{1\}}$,
$Z_\beta=2^{\beta-1}$ and $R_\beta=R$. With $t=2$, $E_1:=R_\beta(X_1)$ and
\[
   E_2:=R_\beta(X_2)\mathbf 1_{\{X_1=1\}}+\mathbf 1_{\{X_1=0\}} ,
\]
which is a legitimate betting sequence, one has $W_2=4$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s., hence
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[W_2^{-s}]=4^{-s}=e^{-2\lambda(\beta)}$ and $\Lambda^{(2)}_s=\lambda(\beta)$:
equality holds, although $\mathbb{P}_0(E_2\ne R_\beta(X_2))=\frac12$. Under
$P_0\sim P_1$ the two conclusions coincide.
<!-- end remark-12 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:ceiling}
For every betting sequence, every $s\in[0,\infty)$ and every $t\in\mathbb{N}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ceiling}
   \Lambda^{(t)}_s\ \le\ \frac1t\sum_{n\le t}\ \bar\lambda_n(0^{+}),
   \qquad
   \bar\lambda_n(0^{+}):=\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{\mathbb{P}_1}\ \lambda_n(0^{+}) ,
\end{equation}
with $\lambda_n(0^{+})$ as in \Cref{lem:Zf-cond}(ii); the same bound therefore
holds for $\Lambda^{(t)}$. The quantity being averaged is a divergence:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:lambda0-is-kl}
   \lambda_n(0^{+})\ =\ \overline{\mathrm{KL}}_n\ :=\ -\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}\left[\log R_n\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}\right] ,
\end{equation}
the conditional relative entropy of $\mathbb{P}_0$ with respect to $\mathbb{P}_1$ over
step $n$ (\Cref{lem:limit-cond}), so \eqref{eq:ceiling} caps the exponent by the
average of the first $t$ per-step conditional Chernoff--Stein exponents. In the
i.i.d.\ model the right-hand side is
$\lim_{\beta\downarrow0}\lambda(\beta)=\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$, so
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ceiling-iid}
   \Lambda^{(t)}_s\ \le\ \mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1) ,
\end{equation}
and in particular $\Lambda(E)\le\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$ for every $E\in\mathcal{E}$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
For $s=0$ the left-hand side is $0$ and the right-hand side is nonnegative by
\Cref{lem:Zf-cond}(i). For $s>0$ put $\beta=\frac1{1+s}\in(0,1)$. By
\Cref{lem:Zf-cond}(ii), $\lambda_n(\beta)\le\lambda_n(0^{+})\le\bar\lambda_n(0^{+})$
$\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s., and the right-hand bound is a constant; so
\Cref{prp:upper-seq}\ref{it:agg-det} applies with
$\bar\lambda_n(\beta)=\bar\lambda_n(0^{+})$ and gives \eqref{eq:ceiling}. Taking
the supremum over $s$ gives the statement for $\Lambda^{(t)}$.

In the i.i.d.\ model $\lambda_n(0^{+})=\lim_{\beta\downarrow0}\lambda(\beta)$ is
the same constant for every $n$, and that limit exists in $[0,\infty]$ by
\Cref{lem:Zf}(ii) and equals $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$ by \Cref{lem:limit}; the last claim
is \Cref{lem:iidexp}. Identity \eqref{eq:lambda0-is-kl} is \Cref{lem:limit-cond}.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- remark-13: body_md -->
\label{rem:generalceiling}
\Cref{cor:ceiling} holds on any filtered space: no product structure, no
stationarity, no identically distributed anything. Three things about it are
settled elsewhere, and it is worth saying where.

\emph{It is a divergence, up to an essential supremum.} By
\eqref{eq:lambda0-is-kl} each $\lambda_n(0^{+})$ is a conditional relative
entropy, so \eqref{eq:ceiling} is the Ces\`aro average of their essential
suprema, and in particular
$\frac1t\sum_{n\le t}\bar\lambda_n(0^{+})
\ge\frac1t\mathrm{KL}(\mathbb{P}_0|_{\mathcal{F}_t}\|\mathbb{P}_1|_{\mathcal{F}_t})$ by \Cref{lem:compensator}.
The two sides agree when the $\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_n$ are $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.\ constant
(\Cref{ass:homog}), and then the average is the predictable compensator of
$-\frac1t\log L_t$ exactly. Whether it converges as $t\to\infty$ is a property
of the model, not of the method: it does for stationary ergodic pairs, where the
limit is the relative entropy rate, and it can fail for independent but
non-identically distributed ones (\Cref{rem:rate}).

\emph{It is tight, but not for free.} A witness exists in full generality: the
predictable flattened design $R_{\beta,n}$ of \Cref{def:flat-cond} attains the
per-step bound with no extra hypothesis (\Cref{lem:flat-cond}). What is needed
for the per-step values to aggregate into a deterministic total is that they be
non-random (\Cref{ass:homog}); under that hypothesis
\Cref{thm:ceiling-gen} matches \eqref{eq:ceiling}, and under its further
non-degeneracy hypotheses shows the value is not attained. In the i.i.d.\ model
\Cref{ass:homog} is automatic, the total is $t\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$, and the matched
statement is \Cref{thm:ceiling}. Without \Cref{ass:homog} the sharpness of
\eqref{eq:ceiling} is open: the essential suprema may be strict, and we know of
no matching example.

\emph{It bounds the exponent, not yet the error.} \eqref{eq:ceiling} caps
$\Lambda^{(t)}$, which enters the error only through \Cref{lem:chernoff}. That
the same ceiling binds the type-II error itself is \Cref{prp:stein-ceiling} in
the i.i.d.\ model, and \Cref{prp:stein-gen} in general, under an
information-spectrum hypothesis on $-\frac1t\log L_t$ (\Cref{ass:spectrum});
\Cref{prp:rate} identifies its constant with the same average, under a
conditional-variance bound.

\emph{And the dichotomy generalises for free.} The \textsf{e}-power{} side of
\Cref{thm:two} needs no extra hypothesis at all: by \Cref{lem:epower-cond} the
conditional \textsf{e}-power{} of any bet is at most the conditional relative entropy
$\mathrm{KL}_n$ in the opposite direction, with equality if and only if $E_n=R_n$. So on
any filtered space the two ceilings are the two conditional divergences, one
attained step by step by the likelihood ratio and one not.

\Cref{app:general} carries all of this out.
<!-- end remark-13 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prp:stein-ceiling}
Work in the i.i.d.\ model (\Cref{def:iid}) and assume $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)<\infty$.
For every betting sequence and every
$\alpha\in(0,1)$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:stein-ceiling}
   \limsup_{t\to\infty}\ -\frac1t\log\bar\gamma_t(\alpha)
   \ \le\ \mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1),
\end{equation}
and the same holds with $\gamma_t(\alpha)$ in place of $\bar\gamma_t(\alpha)$.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Fix $t$ and put $C_t:=\{\tau_\alpha>t\}$. Then $C_t\in\mathcal{F}_t=\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{X}}^{\otimes t}$,
and $P_0^{\otimes t}(C_t^{c})=\mathbb{P}_0(\tau_\alpha\le t)\le
\mathbb{P}_0(\tau_\alpha<\infty)\le\alpha$ by \Cref{thm:typeI}, so $C_t$ is an
admissible acceptance region in the Chernoff--Stein lemma, whose value
$\gamma^{\star}_t(\alpha)$ is the least type-II error of any test of level
$\alpha$ at horizon $t$
\cite{Chernoff56}, \cite[Thm.~11.8.3]{CT06}, \cite{HK89}
(\Cref{thm:app-stein}). Its type-II error is
$P_1^{\otimes t}(C_t)=\bar\gamma_t(\alpha)$, whence
$\bar\gamma_t(\alpha)\ge\gamma^{\star}_t(\alpha)$ and
$-\frac1t\log\bar\gamma_t(\alpha)\le-\frac1t\log\gamma^{\star}_t(\alpha)$. Let
$t\to\infty$ and apply \Cref{thm:app-stein}; the range-free form quoted there
(valid for every $\alpha\in(0,1)$ by the strong converse of \cite{HK89}) is what
lets $\alpha$ be arbitrary. For $\gamma_t(\alpha)$ take
instead $C_t:=\{W_t\le\frac1\alpha\}\in\mathcal{F}_t$, whose type-I error
$\mathbb{P}_0(W_t>\frac1\alpha)\le\alpha\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[W_t]\le\alpha$ by Markov.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:limit}
$\displaystyle\lim_{\beta\downarrow0}\lambda(\beta)=\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$, in $[0,\infty]$.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
For $\beta\in(0,1]$ define $h_\beta:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}$ by
$h_\beta:=\frac{R^{\beta}-1}{\beta}$. Three observations.

\emph{(a) Monotone decrease.} For fixed $x\in[0,\infty)$ the map
$\beta\mapsto\frac{x^{\beta}-1}{\beta}$ is nondecreasing on $(0,1]$. For $x>0$
it is the difference quotient at $0$ of the convex map
$\beta\mapsto e^{\beta\log x}$, hence nondecreasing for every value of
$\log x\in\mathbb{R}$; for $x=0$ it equals $-\frac1\beta$, which is nondecreasing. In
both cases it decreases to $\log x\in[-\infty,\infty)$ as $\beta\downarrow0$.
Hence $h_\beta\downarrow\log R$ pointwise.

\emph{(b) An integrable majorant.} By (a), $h_\beta\le h_1=R-1$ for all
$\beta\in(0,1]$, and $\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[|R-1|]\le2<\infty$.

\emph{(c) Passing to the limit.} By monotone convergence for the decreasing
family $(h_\beta)_{\beta\in(0,1]}$ dominated above by the integrable $R-1$,
\[
   \lim_{\beta\downarrow0}\mathbb{E}_{P_0}\left[ h_\beta\right]
   =\mathbb{E}_{P_0}\left[\log R\right]=-\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)\in[-\infty,0] ,
\]
the last equality because $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)=\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[\log\frac{dP_0}{dP_1}]
=-\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[\log R]$ when $P_0\ll P_1$, and both sides are $+\infty$ otherwise.

Now $\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[h_\beta]=\frac{Z_\beta-1}{\beta}$ and
$\lambda(\beta)=-\frac{\log Z_\beta}{\beta}$. If $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)<\infty$ then
$Z_\beta\to1$, so $\log Z_\beta=(Z_\beta-1)(1+o(1))$ and
$\lambda(\beta)=-\frac{Z_\beta-1}{\beta}(1+o(1))\to\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$. If
$\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)=\infty$ then $\frac{Z_\beta-1}{\beta}\to-\infty$; since
$\log y\le y-1$ for $y>0$ we get $\lambda(\beta)\ge-\frac{Z_\beta-1}{\beta}\to\infty$.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lem:flat}
For every $\beta\in(0,1]$: $R_\beta\in\mathcal{E}$ with $\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[R_\beta]=1$, and with
$s=\frac{1-\beta}{\beta}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:flat-attains}
   \Lambda_{s}(R_\beta)\ =\ \lambda(\beta),
   \qquad\text{hence}\qquad
   \Lambda(R_\beta)\ \ge\ \lambda(\beta) .
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
$\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[R_\beta]=\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[R^{\beta}]/Z_\beta=1$, so $R_\beta\in\mathcal{E}$. For
\eqref{eq:flat-attains} compute directly:
\[
   \mathbb{E}_{P_1}\left[ R_\beta^{-s}\right]
   =Z_\beta^{s}\,\mathbb{E}_{P_1}\left[ R^{-\beta s}\right]
   =Z_\beta^{s}\,\mathbb{E}_{P_0}\left[ R^{1-\beta s}\right] ,
\]
using the change of measure $\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[\varphi(R)]=\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[R\,\varphi(R)]$,
valid for every measurable $\varphi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty]$. Since
$\beta s=1-\beta$ we have
$1-\beta s=\beta$, so $\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[R^{1-\beta s}]=Z_\beta$ and
\[
   \mathbb{E}_{P_1}\left[ R_\beta^{-s}\right]=Z_\beta^{s+1}=Z_\beta^{1/\beta} ,
\]
because $s+1=\frac{1-\beta}{\beta}+1=\frac1\beta$. Taking $-\log$,
$\Lambda_s(R_\beta)=-\frac1\beta\log Z_\beta=\lambda(\beta)$. The inequality follows
from $\Lambda(R_\beta)=\sup_{s'\ge0}\Lambda_{s'}(R_\beta)\ge\Lambda_s(R_\beta)$.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:chernoffinfo}
Under \Cref{ass:standing} with $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)<\infty$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:chernoffinfo}
   \Lambda(R)\ =\ \sup_{\beta\in(0,1]}\beta\,\lambda(\beta)
   \ =\ -\inf_{\beta\in(0,1]}\log Z_\beta\ =\ C(P_0,P_1) ,
\end{equation}
the Chernoff information of the pair. Moreover, if $\log R$ is not $P_0$-a.s.\
constant then $\Lambda(R_\beta)>\lambda(\beta)$ strictly, for every
$\beta\in(0,1]$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
For $s\ge0$, the change of measure $\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[\varphi(R)]=\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[R\,\varphi(R)]$
gives $\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[R^{-s}]=\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[R^{1-s}]=Z_{1-s}$ when $s\in[0,1)$, so
\[
   \Lambda_s(R)=-\log Z_{1-s} ;
\]
valid for every $s\ge0$ because $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)<\infty$ gives $P_0(R>0)=1$, so
that $R>0$ holds $P_0$-a.s.\ as well as $P_1$-a.s. Substituting $\beta=1-s$
turns $\sup_{s\ge0}$ into $\sup_{\beta\le1}$ of $-\log Z_\beta$. The map
$\beta\mapsto\log Z_\beta$ is convex with $Z_0=Z_1=1$, so $-\log Z_\beta\le0$
for $\beta\le0$ while $-\log Z_\beta\ge0$ on $[0,1]$; the supremum is therefore
attained on $(0,1]$ and equals $\sup_{\beta\in(0,1]}\beta\lambda(\beta)$. The
last equality is the definition of the Chernoff information. For the strictness, write
$dP_\beta:=R_\beta\,dP_0$; differentiating $\sigma\mapsto\Lambda_\sigma(R_\beta)$
at the paired tilt $\sigma=s=\frac{1-\beta}{\beta}$ gives
\[
   \frac{d}{d\sigma}\Lambda_\sigma(R_\beta)\Big|_{\sigma=s}
   =\frac{\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[R_\beta^{-s}\log R_\beta]}{\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[R_\beta^{-s}]}
   =\mathrm{KL}(P_\beta\|P_0)\ >\ 0 ,
\]
the last inequality because $P_\beta=P_0$ would force $R^{\beta}$ to be
$P_0$-a.s.\ constant. So $\Lambda(R_\beta)\ge\Lambda_{\sigma}(R_\beta)>
\Lambda_s(R_\beta)=\lambda(\beta)$ for $\sigma$ slightly above $s$.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- remark-14: body_md -->
\label{rem:three}
\eqref{eq:chernoffinfo} identifies the exponent of the growth-optimal design in
closed form whenever $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)<\infty$: it is the Chernoff information, the
largest rectangle $\beta\times\lambda(\beta)$ under the curve of
\Cref{fig:two}. The subject therefore has three named constants,
\[
   C(P_0,P_1)\ \le\ \min\left\{\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0),\ \mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)\right\} :
\]
the exponent $C(P_0,P_1)$ of the \textsf{e}-power{}-optimal design; the \textsf{e}-power{} ceiling
$\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)$, which that design attains; and the exponent ceiling
$\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$, which no design attains. The last two are not comparable with
each other (\Cref{rem:notcomparable}).
<!-- end remark-14 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:lower}
$\displaystyle\sup_{E\in\mathcal{E}}\Lambda(E)\ \ge\ \mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
By \Cref{lem:flat}, $\sup_{E\in\mathcal{E}}\Lambda(E)\ge\sup_{\beta\in(0,1]}\lambda(\beta)
=\lim_{\beta\downarrow0}\lambda(\beta)$, the equality by monotonicity
(\Cref{lem:Zf}(ii)); and that limit is $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$ by \Cref{lem:limit}.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- remark-15: body_md -->
\label{rem:whatgeneralises}
The upper half of this section is stated in the setting of \Cref{def:setting}:
\Cref{thm:upper-cond}, \Cref{prp:upper-seq}\ref{it:agg-exact}--\ref{it:agg-det}
and \Cref{cor:ceiling} use only that $\mathbb{P}_0,\mathbb{P}_1$ are laws on a filtered
space with $\mathbb{P}_1\ll\mathbb{P}_0$ on each $\mathcal{F}_t$. So do
\Cref{def:cond-evar}--\Cref{lem:order}, \Cref{lem:chernoff}, and
\Cref{sec:nfl} apart from \Cref{rem:quantifier}, \Cref{prp:powerone} and
\Cref{rem:cramer}, which name the i.i.d.\ model. What the general form gives up is that the ceiling is no longer
one number: it is the average $\frac1t\sum_{n\le t}\bar\lambda_n(0^{+})$ of
per-step conditional Chernoff--Stein exponents, and \Cref{cor:ceiling} must pass
to an essential supremum to make the per-step bounds aggregate.

Three things below genuinely use more. The lower bound needs a witness
whose per-step value is non-random, which is what lets the
per-step bounds aggregate deterministically; \Cref{prp:stein-ceiling} invokes the
Chernoff--Stein lemma, an i.i.d.\ statement; and \Cref{sec:horizon} rests on the
identity of \Cref{prp:exactfamily}, which requires $Z_{\beta,n}$ to be
deterministic and constant in $n$. The equality analysis of
\Cref{thm:upper}, and hence \Cref{prp:upper-seq}\ref{it:agg-iid} and
\Cref{prp:notattained}, is stated in the i.i.d.\ model for a different reason:
the conditional H\"older equality case carries an $\mathcal{F}_{n-1}$-measurable
proportionality factor, and identifying it is what the sections argument does.

\Cref{app:general} carries each of these out: it states the replacement for
each i.i.d.-model result of the main text, together with the hypothesis it
needs, and \Cref{tab:general} is the index; \Cref{rem:generalceiling} summarises
what the general ceiling does and does not settle. Three of them --- the conditional \textsf{e}-power{}
ceiling, the conditional flattened design, and the equality case --- need no
extra hypothesis at all.
<!-- end remark-15 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{lem:attained}
Assume in addition to \Cref{ass:standing} that $P_0\ll P_1$, so that
$P_0\sim P_1$. Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a betting sequence and $t\in\mathbb{N}$ with
$\mathbb{P}_0(W_t\ne1)>0$. Then there is $s^{\ast}\in[0,\infty)$ with
$\Lambda^{(t)}=\Lambda^{(t)}_{s^{\ast}}$.
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
First, $\mathbb{P}_1(W_t<1)>0$. Indeed, suppose $\mathbb{P}_1(W_t<1)=0$, i.e.\ $W_t\ge1$
$\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.; since $P_0\sim P_1$ gives $\mathbb{P}_0|_{\mathcal{F}_t}\sim\mathbb{P}_1|_{\mathcal{F}_t}$
and $W_t$ is $\mathcal{F}_t$-measurable, this gives $W_t\ge1$ $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s., hence
$1\ge\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[W_t]\ge1$ by the supermartingale property, so
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[W_t-1]=0$ with $W_t-1\ge0$ $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s., i.e.\ $W_t=1$
$\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s., contradicting the hypothesis.

Let $\delta:=\mathbb{P}_1(W_t<1)>0$ and pick $\epsilon\in(0,1)$ with
$\mathbb{P}_1(W_t\le1-\epsilon)\ge\delta/2$, possible since
$\{W_t<1\}=\bigcup_{k}\{W_t\le1-\frac1k\}$. Then for $s\ge0$,
\[
   \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}\left[ W_t^{-s}\right]\ \ge\ (1-\epsilon)^{-s}\,\tfrac\delta2
   \ \xrightarrow[s\to\infty]{}\ \infty ,
\]
so $\Lambda^{(t)}_s\to-\infty$. Since $\Lambda^{(t)}_0=0$, there is $S<\infty$
with $\Lambda^{(t)}_s<0$ for all $s>S$, hence
$\Lambda^{(t)}=\sup_{s\in[0,S]}\Lambda^{(t)}_s$. Finally, $W_t<\infty$
$\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.\ (\Cref{lem:supmg} and \Cref{ass:standing}), so for $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.e.\
$\omega$ the map $s\mapsto W_t(\omega)^{-s}$ is lower semicontinuous on
$[0,\infty)$: it is continuous where $W_t(\omega)\in(0,\infty)$, and where
$W_t(\omega)=0$ it equals $1$ at $s=0$ and $+\infty$ for $s>0$. By Fatou's
lemma $s\mapsto\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[W_t^{-s}]$ is then lower semicontinuous, so
$s\mapsto\Lambda^{(t)}_s$ is upper semicontinuous on the compact $[0,S]$ and
attains its supremum there.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- remark-16: body_md -->
\label{rem:whyfatou}
The map $s\mapsto\log\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[W_t^{-s}]$ is convex, but convexity alone
would not close the argument above: a convex function into $(-\infty,\infty]$
can fail to be lower semicontinuous at the endpoint of its effective domain,
which is exactly where the supremum may sit.
<!-- end remark-16 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prp:notattained}
Assume $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)<\infty$ --- which with \Cref{ass:standing} already gives
$P_0\sim P_1$ --- and $P_0\ne P_1$, equivalently that $\log R$ is not
$P_0$-a.s.\ constant. Then
\[
   \Lambda^{(t)}\ <\ \mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)
   \qquad\text{for every betting sequence and every }t\in\mathbb{N} ;
\]
in particular $\Lambda(E)<\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$ for every $E\in\mathcal{E}$.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
If $W_t=1$ $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s.\ then $\Lambda^{(t)}_s=0$ for every $s$, so
$\Lambda^{(t)}=0<\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$, the last inequality because $\log R$ is not
$P_0$-a.s.\ constant, so $P_0\ne P_1$. Otherwise \Cref{lem:attained} gives
$s^{\ast}\in[0,\infty)$ with $\Lambda^{(t)}=\Lambda^{(t)}_{s^{\ast}}$. If
$s^{\ast}=0$ then $\Lambda^{(t)}=0<\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$. If $s^{\ast}>0$ then
\Cref{prp:upper-seq} gives $\Lambda^{(t)}\le \lambda(\beta^{\ast})$ with
$\beta^{\ast}=\frac1{1+s^{\ast}}\in(0,1)$, and \Cref{lem:Zf}(iv) gives
$\lambda(\beta^{\ast})<\lim_{\beta\downarrow0}\lambda(\beta)=\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$ since $\lambda$ is
strictly decreasing. For the last clause take the i.i.d.\ product generated by
$E$ at $t=1$, where $W_1=E$ and $\Lambda^{(1)}=\Lambda(E)$: if $E=1$ $P_0$-a.s.\
then $\Lambda(E)=0<\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$, and otherwise $\mathbb{P}_0(W_1\ne1)>0$.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:ceiling}
Work in the i.i.d.\ model of \Cref{def:iid}. Let $\mathcal W$ denote the class of all betting sequences (equivalently, of all
test supermartingale s) for $\mathbb{P}_0$, and $\mathcal W_{\mathrm{iid}}\subseteq\mathcal W$ the
subclass of i.i.d.\ products generated by a single $E\in\mathcal{E}$. Under
\Cref{ass:standing}, for every $t\in\mathbb{N}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:matched}
   \sup_{\mathcal W}\ \Lambda^{(t)}
   \ =\ \sup_{\mathcal W_{\mathrm{iid}}}\ \Lambda^{(t)}
   \ =\ \sup_{E\in\mathcal{E}}\ \Lambda(E)
   \ =\ \mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1) ,
\end{equation}
the common value being approached along the flattened family
$(R_\beta)_{\beta\in(0,1]}$ of \Cref{def:flattened} as $\beta\downarrow0$. If
moreover $P_0\sim P_1$, $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)<\infty$, and $\log R$ is not $P_0$-a.s.\
constant, then no member of $\mathcal W$ attains it.

Consequently, for every betting sequence, every $\alpha\in(0,1)$ and every
$t\in\mathbb{N}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:matched-error}
   \bar\gamma_t(\alpha)\ \le\ \gamma_t(\alpha)
   \ \le\ \exp\left( s\ell-t\,\Lambda^{(t)}_s\right)
   \quad\text{for all }s\ge0,
\end{equation}
and no betting sequence makes the exponent $\Lambda^{(t)}_s$ exceed
$\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$, for any $s$ and any $t$.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
$\sup_{\mathcal W}\Lambda^{(t)}\le\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$ is \Cref{cor:ceiling}, and
$\sup_{\mathcal W_{\mathrm{iid}}}\Lambda^{(t)}=\sup_{E\in\mathcal{E}}\Lambda(E)\ge
\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$ is \Cref{lem:iidexp} with \Cref{cor:lower}; since
$\mathcal W_{\mathrm{iid}}\subseteq\mathcal W$ the three suprema are squeezed
together. Non-attainment is \Cref{prp:notattained};
\eqref{eq:matched-error} is \Cref{lem:chernoff}; the final clause is
\Cref{cor:ceiling}.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- remark-17: body_md -->
\label{rem:scope}
The two halves of \eqref{eq:matched} have different scopes, and that asymmetry
is the content of the theorem. The upper bound holds for every test supermartingale{}: the
predictable form \Cref{prp:upper-seq} applies \Cref{thm:upper-cond} once per step,
conditionally on the past, so adaptivity buys nothing at all --- and by
\Cref{prp:stein-ceiling} the same ceiling binds the type-II error itself and
not merely the Chernoff bound on it. The lower bound is attained already in the
smallest natural subclass, the i.i.d.\ products of a single \textsf{e}-variable{}. Enlarging
the class from $\mathcal W_{\mathrm{iid}}$ to $\mathcal W$ therefore does not
raise the achievable exponent by so much as an $\epsilon$; and by the equality
case of \Cref{prp:upper-seq}, the only betting sequence achieving the bound
$\lambda(\beta)$ at a given tilt is, up to $\mathbb{P}_1$-null modification, the i.i.d.\
product of $R_\beta$.
<!-- end remark-17 -->
<!-- remark-18: body_md -->
\label{rem:stein}
$\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$ is the Chernoff--Stein exponent: the optimal type-II error
exponent among all tests, sequential or not, whose type-I error is at most a
fixed $\alpha$ \cite{Chernoff56}, \cite[Thm.~11.8.3]{CT06}
(\Cref{thm:app-stein}). \Cref{thm:ceiling} therefore says that
the class of test supermartingale s is exponent-optimal as a class, and that --- when
$\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)<\infty$ and $P_0\ne P_1$ --- no member of it attains the ceiling
at any finite horizon $t$. It does not say that no member
approaches it as $t\to\infty$: \Cref{prp:notattained} bounds $\Lambda^{(t)}$ for
each fixed $t$ and says nothing about $\limsup_{t}\Lambda^{(t)}$, which a single
sequence of bets with a tilt $\beta$ decreasing along blocks can drive to
$\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$.
<!-- end remark-18 -->
<!-- remark-19: body_md -->
\label{rem:attribution}
\Cref{lem:Zf}(ii) and \Cref{lem:limit} are, in the R\'enyi form
$\lambda(\beta)=\mathrm{D}_{1-\beta}(P_0\|P_1)$ of \Cref{lem:Zf}(iii), the monotonicity of
R\'enyi divergence in its order and its limit at order one
\cite[Thms.~3 and 5]{vEH14}; we have given direct proofs to keep the
development self-contained. \Cref{thm:upper} with its equality case is the
$\mathcal{E}$-constrained instance of a known variational characterisation of R\'enyi
divergence \cite{Ana18,ACD15}, restated as \Cref{thm:app-variational}. What the two-sided form
\eqref{eq:matched} adds is the identification of the exact range of
$\Lambda$ on $\mathcal{E}$, together with the non-attainment.
<!-- end remark-19 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:two}
Under \Cref{ass:standing}, in the i.i.d.\ model:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),leftmargin=2.4em]
\item $\displaystyle\sup_{E\in\mathcal{E}}\ \mathbb{E}_{P_1}[\log E]\ =\ \mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)$, and the
