      supremum is attained, at $E=R$ and, up to $P_0$-null modification, only
      there;
\item $\displaystyle\sup_{E\in\mathcal{E}}\ \Lambda(E)\ =\ \mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$, and if
      $P_0\sim P_1$, $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)<\infty$ and $\log R$ is not $P_0$-a.s.\
      constant, the supremum is attained by no $E\in\mathcal{E}$ --- indeed by no
      test supermartingale{}, at any horizon.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
(a) is \Cref{lem:epower-welldef} together with its equality case; (b) is
\Cref{thm:ceiling}.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- remark-20: body_md -->
\label{rem:notcomparable}
$\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)$ and $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$ are the same functional evaluated in
opposite orders, and neither dominates the other: for
$P_0=\mathrm{Bern}(\frac12)$ and $P_1=\mathrm{Bern}(0.99)$ one has
$\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)=1.6145$ and $\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)=0.6371$, a ratio of $2.53$, and
exchanging the two hypotheses reverses it. (We assume here, as in \Cref{thm:two}(b), that
$\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)<\infty$ and $P_0\ne P_1$. Without them both suprema can be
attained by the same \textsf{e}-variable{} --- in the model of \Cref{rem:eqcase},
$P_0=\mathrm{Bern}(\frac12)$ and $P_1=\delta_1$, one has $\Lambda(R)=\infty=
\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$, and $R$ maximises both scalars.) So neither ceiling dominates
the other, and which is the larger depends on the model. They may of course also
coincide: in the Gaussian location model of \Cref{ex:gauss} both equal
$\Delta^{2}/2$. What \Cref{thm:two} asserts is not that the two values always
differ, but that the two \emph{optimisation problems} do --- different
maximisers, and one supremum attained where the other is not.
<!-- end remark-20 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{ex:ceiling}
Let $\mathcal{X}=\{0,1\}$, $P_0=\mathrm{Bern}(\frac12)$, $P_1=\mathrm{Bern}(0.6)$, so
$R(1)=1.2$ and $R(0)=0.8$. Then
\[
   \mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)=\tfrac12\log\tfrac{0.5}{0.6}+\tfrac12\log\tfrac{0.5}{0.4}
   =0.0204110 ,
\]
and $Z_\beta=\frac12(1.2^{\beta}+0.8^{\beta})$, $\lambda(\beta)=-\beta^{-1}\log Z_\beta$:
\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcccccc@{}}
\toprule
$\beta$ & $1$ & $0.5$ & $0.25$ & $0.1$ & $0.05$ & $\downarrow0$\\
\midrule
$\lambda(\beta)$ & $0$ & $0.0101534$ & $0.0152756$ & $0.0183561$ & $0.0193835$
   & $0.0204110$\\
$\Lambda(R_\beta)$ & $0.0050768$ & $0.0114340$ & $0.0155965$ & $0.0184075$
   & $0.0193963$ & $0.0204110$\\
$\Lambda(R_\beta)$ as \% of $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$ & $24.9$ & $56.0$ & $76.4$ & $90.2$
   & $95.0$ & $100$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\Cref{lem:flat} gives $\Lambda_s(R_\beta)=\lambda(\beta)$ at the paired tilt
$s=\frac{1-\beta}{\beta}$, hence $\Lambda(R_\beta)\ge\lambda(\beta)$; the second
row shows the inequality is strict, as \Cref{cor:chernoffinfo} explains. The
columns $\beta=0.1$ and $\beta=0.05$ exhibit \textsf{e}-variables{} whose exponent is within
$10\%$, respectively $5\%$, of the ceiling, and by \Cref{prp:notattained} no
\textsf{e}-variable{} reaches $0.0204110$. The last column is a limit, not an \textsf{e}-variable{}.

The likelihood ratio itself, $E=R=R_1$, has
\[
   \Lambda(R)=\sup_{s\ge0}\left\{-\log\left(0.6\cdot1.2^{-s}+0.4\cdot0.8^{-s}\right)\right\}
   =0.0050768 ,
\]
attained at $s^{\ast}=0.5017$, which is $24.9\%$ of the ceiling. The tilt that
\Cref{thm:upper} pairs with this $s^{\ast}$ is
$\beta^{\ast}=\frac1{1+s^{\ast}}=0.6659$, and the bound it gives is
\[
   \Lambda(R)=\Lambda_{s^{\ast}}(R)=0.0050768\ <\ \lambda(\beta^{\ast})=0.0067677 ,
\]
strictly, as it must be by the equality case of \Cref{thm:upper}: $R$ is not
equal to $R^{\beta^{\ast}}/Z_{\beta^{\ast}}$. So the \textsf{e}-variable{} of maximal
\textsf{e}-power{} --- $\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[\log R]=\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)=0.0201355$, the largest possible by
\Cref{lem:epower-welldef} --- realises barely a quarter of the largest possible
exponent, and is beaten already by the single flattening
$R_{\beta^{\ast}}$. The two scalars of \Cref{rem:two-scalars} are maximised by
different \textsf{e}-variables{}.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{lem:family}
For $\beta\in\mathcal{B}$ let $R_\beta$ be as in \Cref{def:flattened} and put
$c_\beta:=\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[\log R_\beta]$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cbeta}
   c_\beta\ =\ \beta\left(\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)+\lambda(\beta)\right) ,
\end{equation}
and, assuming $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)<\infty$ and $\log R$ not $P_0$-a.s.\ constant:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.4em]
\item $\beta\mapsto c_\beta$ is strictly increasing on $(0,1)$ and strictly
      decreasing on $(1,\beta_{\max})$, with $c_{0^{+}}=0$ and maximum
      $c_1=\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)$;
\item $\beta\mapsto\lambda(\beta)$ is strictly decreasing on
      $\mathcal{B}$, with $\lambda(0^{+})=\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$, $\lambda(1)=0$
      and $\lambda(\beta)<0$ for $\beta>1$;
\item $c_\beta/\beta\uparrow\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)+\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)$, the Jeffreys
      divergence, as $\beta\downarrow0$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
Write $\kappa(\beta):=\log Z_\beta$, so $\lambda(\beta)=-\kappa(\beta)/\beta$.
Then $\log R_\beta=\beta\log R-\kappa(\beta)$, and taking $\mathbb{E}_{P_1}$ gives
$c_\beta=\beta\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)-\kappa(\beta)=\beta\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)+\beta\lambda(\beta)$,
which is \eqref{eq:cbeta}. The map $\kappa$ is the cumulant generating function
of $\log R$ under $P_0$, hence convex. Note first that $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)<\infty$
forces $P_0(R>0)=1$, so $Z_\beta\to P_0(R>0)=1$ and $\kappa(0^{+})=0$; also
$\kappa(1)=\log\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[R]=0$. Thus $\kappa(0^{+})=\kappa(1)=0$,
$\kappa'(0^{+})=\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[\log R]=-\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$ and
$\kappa'(1)=\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[R\log R]=\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)$, the latter a left derivative,
since $Z_\beta$ may be infinite for every $\beta>1$; the interchange
$\frac{d}{d\beta}\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[R^{\beta}]=\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[R^{\beta}\log R]$ at $\beta\uparrow1$
is legitimate by monotone convergence on $\{R\ge1\}$ (where
$\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[(R\log R)_+]<\infty$ by \Cref{ass:standing}) and dominated convergence
on $\{R<1\}$ (where $R^{\beta}|\log R|\le1/(e\beta_0)$ for $\beta\ge\beta_0>0$).
The value $\kappa'(0^{+})=-\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$ is not the same interchange: it is
$\lim_{\beta\downarrow0}\kappa(\beta)/\beta=-\lim_{\beta\downarrow0}\lambda(\beta)$
by convexity, and \Cref{lem:limit}. Finally $\kappa$ is strictly convex because
$\log R$ is not $P_0$-a.s.\ constant \emph{and}, by the previous sentence,
$P_0(R>0)=1$, so that $\kappa''(\beta)=\operatorname{Var}_{P_\beta}(\log R)>0$ for the tilt
$dP_\beta\propto R^{\beta}dP_0$. For (i),
$\frac{d}{d\beta}c_\beta=\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)-\kappa'(\beta)$, and $\kappa'$ is
strictly increasing with $\kappa'(1)=\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)$, so the derivative is
strictly positive on $(0,1)$, vanishes at $\beta=1$ and is strictly negative on
$(1,\beta_{\max})$; the values are $c_1=\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)$ and $c_{0^{+}}=0$. For
(ii), $\lambda(\beta)=-\kappa(\beta)/\beta$ is minus the slope of the chord of
$\kappa$ from $0$ to $\beta$, which is strictly increasing on all of
$\mathcal{B}$ because $\kappa$ is strictly convex with $\kappa(0^{+})=0$;
the two values are \Cref{lem:limit} and $\kappa(1)=0$, and $\lambda(\beta)<0$
for $\beta>1$ because $\kappa(\beta)>0$ there. For
(iii), $c_\beta/\beta=\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)+\lambda(\beta)$ by \eqref{eq:cbeta}, and
$\lambda(\beta)$ increases to $\lambda(0^{+})=\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$ as
$\beta\downarrow0$ by (ii).
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- remark-21: body_md -->
\label{rem:familypicture}
\Cref{lem:family} is the two ceilings in one curve. At $\beta=1$ the design is
$R$: \textsf{e}-power{} maximal, exponent $\lambda(1)=0$ from this bound. As $\beta$
decreases the \textsf{e}-power{} falls monotonically to $0$ while the tilt-$\beta$
exponent $\lambda(\beta)$ rises monotonically to $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$. No member of the family is good at both, and
\Cref{thm:two} shows that the two objectives are maximised at different places
and that one supremum is attained where the other is not, and \Cref{fig:two}
plots the trade-off along the family for the model of \Cref{ex:ceiling}. We do
not prove a quantitative trade-off valid for arbitrary \textsf{e}-variables{}; along the
family it can be read off the figure.
<!-- end remark-21 -->
<!-- definition-15: body_md -->
\label{def:GB}
Put
\[
   G_\bullet:\mathbb{N}_0\times\Omega\to[-\infty,\infty),\qquad
   G_t:=\sum_{n=1}^{t}\log R(X_n),\qquad G_0:=0,
\]
and
\[
   B_\bullet(\beta):\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R},\qquad
   B_t(\beta):=\frac{\ell}{\beta}-t\,\lambda(\beta) .
\]
<!-- end definition-15 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{lem:surrogate}
For every $\beta\in\mathcal{B}$, $\alpha\in(0,1)$ and $t\in\mathbb{N}$, the i.i.d.\ product
generated by $R_\beta$ satisfies $\gamma_t(\alpha)\le e^{B_t(\beta)}$.
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
$R_\beta^{-1/\beta}=Z_\beta^{1/\beta}R^{-1}$, and
$\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[R^{-1}]=\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[R\cdot R^{-1}]=P_0(R>0)\le1$, so
$\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[R_\beta^{-1/\beta}]\le Z_\beta^{1/\beta}=e^{-\lambda(\beta)}$, i.e.\
$\Lambda_{1/\beta}(R_\beta)\ge\lambda(\beta)$. \Cref{lem:chernoff} at
$s=\frac1\beta$ then gives
$\gamma_t(\alpha)\le\exp(\frac{\ell}{\beta}-t\lambda(\beta))=e^{B_t(\beta)}$.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prp:exactfamily}
Fix $\beta\in\mathcal{B}$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$, and let $(W_t)_{t\in\mathbb{N}_0}$ be the
i.i.d.\ product generated by $R_\beta$. Then for every $t\in\mathbb{N}$:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),leftmargin=2.4em]
\item $\log W_t=\beta\left( G_t-B_t(\beta)\right)+\ell$, and consequently
      \begin{equation}\label{eq:exactgamma}
         \gamma_t(\alpha)=\mathbb{P}_1\left( G_t\le B_t(\beta)\right),
         \qquad
         \bar\gamma_t(\alpha)
            =\mathbb{P}_1\left( G_n\le B_n(\beta)\ \text{for all }n\le t\right) ;
      \end{equation}
\item the whole family $(R_\beta)_{\beta\in\mathcal{B}}$ therefore performs the
      \emph{same} test --- reject when the log-likelihood-ratio sum $G_t$
      exceeds a threshold --- and differs only in where the threshold is put;
\item $\gamma_t(\alpha)\ \ge\ \mathbb{P}_1\left( G_t\le\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[G_t]\right)$ whenever
      $t\,c_\beta\le\ell$ --- in particular at every $t$ when $c_\beta\le0$ ---
      with $c_\beta$ as in \Cref{lem:family}; and the
      surrogate bound $e^{B_t(\beta)}$ of \Cref{lem:surrogate} is vacuous
      unless $\lambda(\beta)>0$ --- that is, unless $\beta<1$ --- and
      $t>\ell/(\beta\lambda(\beta))$. (The Chernoff bound of
      \Cref{lem:chernoff} at $s=\frac1\beta$ is $e^{B_t(\beta)}P_0(R>0)^{t}$,
      which is smaller when $P_0(R>0)<1$; the two agree under
      $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)<\infty$.)
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
(a) $\log R_\beta=\beta\log R-\log Z_\beta$ and $-\log Z_\beta=\beta\lambda(\beta)$,
so $\log W_t=\beta G_t+t\beta\lambda(\beta)
=\beta\left( G_t-\frac{\ell}{\beta}+t\lambda(\beta)\right)+\ell
=\beta(G_t-B_t(\beta))+\ell$. Hence $W_t\le\frac1\alpha$, i.e.\
$\log W_t\le\ell$, holds precisely when $G_t\le B_t(\beta)$; the second identity
in \eqref{eq:exactgamma} follows by applying this at every $n\le t$ and using
$\{\tau_\alpha>t\}=\bigcap_{n\le t}\{W_n\le\frac1\alpha\}$. Part (b) restates
(a). For (c), $\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[G_t]=t\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)$, and by \eqref{eq:cbeta}
$B_t(\beta)\ge t\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)$ is equivalent to
$\ell\ge t\beta(\lambda(\beta)+\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0))=t\,c_\beta$; monotonicity of
$x\mapsto\mathbb{P}_1(G_t\le x)$ then gives the stated inequality. The last claim is
$B_t(\beta)\ge0$, i.e.\ $t\lambda(\beta)\le\ell/\beta$.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:betastar}
Assume $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)<\infty$, $\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)<\infty$, and that $\log R$ is not
$P_0$-a.s.\ constant, and write
\[
   g(\beta)\ :=\ \beta\kappa'(\beta)-\kappa(\beta) ,
\]
which is strictly increasing on $\mathcal{B}$ with $g(0^{+})=0$ and
$g(1)=\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)$. For fixed $t$ the map $\beta\mapsto B_t(\beta)$ on
$\mathcal{B}$ is strictly decreasing and then, if $\ell/t$ lies in the
range of $g$, strictly increasing; in that case it has a unique minimiser
$\beta^{\ast}(t)$, characterised by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:betastar-root}
   g\left(\beta^{\ast}(t)\right)\ =\ \frac{\ell}{t} ,
\end{equation}
and otherwise the infimum is approached as $\beta\uparrow\beta_{\max}$. By
\Cref{prp:exactfamily}(a) the minimiser also minimises the exact type-II error
$\gamma_t(\alpha)$ over the family. Moreover:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),leftmargin=2.4em]
\item \emph{(Crossover.)} Whenever $\beta^{\ast}(t)$ exists,
      $\beta^{\ast}(t)\gtreqless1$ according as
      $t\lesseqgtr\ell/\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)$. In particular the growth-optimal design
      $R$ is the horizon-optimal member of the family at exactly one, generally
      non-integer, horizon,
      \[
         t\ =\ \frac{\ell}{\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)} ;
      \]
      below it $R$ is beaten by \emph{sharpening} and above it by
      \emph{flattening}, with $\beta^{\ast}(t)\downarrow0$ as $t\to\infty$.
\item \emph{(Rate.)} Assume in addition that $\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[R^{-\delta}]<\infty$ for
      some $\delta>0$ --- equivalently, $Z_\beta<\infty$ for some $\beta<0$, so
      that $\kappa(\beta)=\log Z_\beta$ is finite, hence real-analytic, on a
      two-sided neighbourhood of $0$ --- and that
      $V_0:=\operatorname{Var}_{P_0}(\log R)=\kappa''(0)\in(0,\infty)$. Then
      \[
         \lambda(\beta)=\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)-\tfrac{V_0}{2}\,\beta+O(\beta^{2})
         \quad(\beta\downarrow0),
         \qquad
         \beta^{\ast}(t)=\sqrt{\frac{2\ell}{t\,V_0}}\,(1+o(1)) ,
      \]
      and, at that tilt,
      \begin{equation}\label{eq:capstone}
         \gamma_t(\alpha)\ \le\
         \exp\left(-t\,\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)+\sqrt{2\,\ell\,t\,V_0}+O(1)\right)
         \qquad(t\to\infty).
      \end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
Since $\lambda'(\beta)=-g(\beta)/\beta^{2}$,
\[
   B_t'(\beta)=-\frac{\ell}{\beta^{2}}-t\,\lambda'(\beta)
   =\frac{t\,g(\beta)-\ell}{\beta^{2}} .
\]
Now $g(0^{+})=0$ --- this is where $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)<\infty$ is consumed, since it
gives both $\kappa(0^{+})=0$ (equivalently $P_0(R>0)=1$) and
$\beta\kappa'(\beta)\to0$ --- and $g'(\beta)=\beta\kappa''(\beta)>0$, since
$\kappa$ is strictly convex; so $g$ is strictly increasing from $0$, and
$g(1)=\kappa'(1)-\kappa(1)=\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)$. Hence $\beta\mapsto t\,g(\beta)-\ell$
changes sign at most once, from negative to positive. If $\ell/t$ lies in the
range of $g$ the sign change occurs at the $\beta$ of
\eqref{eq:betastar-root}, $B_t$ is strictly decreasing and then strictly
increasing, and with $B_t(0^{+})=+\infty$ the minimiser is unique; if not, $B_t$
is strictly decreasing throughout $\mathcal{B}$ and its infimum is approached as
$\beta\uparrow\beta_{\max}$. Since
$\mathbb{P}_1(G_t\le x)$ is nondecreasing in $x$, minimising $B_t$ minimises
$\gamma_t(\alpha)=\mathbb{P}_1(G_t\le B_t(\beta))$ over the family.

(a) Since $g$ is strictly increasing, $\beta^{\ast}(t)=g^{-1}(\ell/t)$ exceeds,
equals or falls below $1$ according as $\ell/t$ exceeds, equals or falls below
$g(1)=\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)$. As $g$ does not depend on $t$, the solution decreases in
$t$, tending to $0$ because $g(0^{+})=0$; and $\ell/t<g(\beta_{\max}^{-})$ holds
for all large $t$, so $\beta^{\ast}(t)$ exists there.

(b) The extra hypothesis makes $\kappa$ finite on $(-\delta,1]$, hence
real-analytic on $(-\delta,1)$, so its Taylor expansion at $0$ carries a genuine
$O(\beta^{3})$ remainder --- which is what the $O(1)$ below needs; with only
$\kappa''(0^{+})$ finite one would get an error $t\cdot o(\beta)=o(\sqrt t)$.
With $\kappa(\beta)=-\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)\beta+\frac{V_0}{2}\beta^{2}+O(\beta^{3})$
we get $\lambda(\beta)=-\kappa(\beta)/\beta=\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)-\frac{V_0}{2}\beta
+O(\beta^{2})$, and $g(\beta)=\beta\kappa'(\beta)-\kappa(\beta)
=\frac{V_0}{2}\beta^{2}+O(\beta^{3})$; solving $t\,g(\beta)=\ell$ gives
$\beta^{\ast}(t)=\sqrt{2\ell/(tV_0)}(1+o(1))$. For \eqref{eq:capstone} we do not need the asymptotics of $\beta^{\ast}(t)$ at
all: since $\beta^{\ast}(t)$ minimises $B_t$, it suffices to evaluate $B_t$ at
the explicit $b_t:=\sqrt{2\ell/(tV_0)}$, which lies in $(0,1]$ for
$t\ge2\ell/V_0$. From
$\lambda(\beta)=\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)-\frac{V_0}{2}\beta+O(\beta^{2})$ and
$t\,b_t^{2}=2\ell/V_0=O(1)$,
\[
   B_t(\beta^{\ast}(t))\ \le\ B_t(b_t)
   =\frac{\ell}{b_t}+\frac{tV_0}{2}b_t-t\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)+O(t\,b_t^{2})
   =-t\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)+\sqrt{2\ell tV_0}+O(1) ,
\]
because $\frac{\ell}{b_t}=\frac{tV_0}{2}b_t=\sqrt{\ell tV_0/2}$.
\Cref{lem:surrogate} gives $\gamma_t(\alpha)\le e^{B_t(\beta)}$ for every
$\beta$; take $\beta=\beta^{\ast}(t)$.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- remark-22: body_md -->
\label{rem:crossover}
The threshold $\ell/\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)$ in \Cref{thm:betastar}(a) is exactly the
number of observations the likelihood ratio needs to accumulate $\ell=\log\frac1\alpha$
nats of evidence \emph{on average}, since $\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[\log R]=\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)$. So
within the family the growth-optimal design is the right one at exactly the
horizon at which it typically rejects, and is improved on to either side of it
--- strictly in the threshold
$B_t$, and hence strictly in the error whenever $\mathbb{P}_1$ charges the interval
$(B_t(\beta^{\ast}(t)),B_t(1)]$. When $\log R$ is lattice-valued the
improvement can lag the threshold: in the model of \Cref{ex:ceiling}, at
$\alpha=0.05$, the crossover is at $t=148.8$, but $G_t$ lives on a lattice of
spacing $\log\frac32$ and the exact errors of $R$ and of $R_{\beta^{\ast}(t)}$
coincide for $t=149,\dots,191$, the first strict improvement occurring at
$t=192$; for larger $t$ they continue to coincide at isolated horizons. That is
the
operational form of \Cref{thm:two}: which ceiling one should be aiming at
depends on how long one is prepared to wait.
<!-- end remark-22 -->
<!-- remark-23: body_md -->
\label{rem:sharpen}
Below the crossover the horizon-optimal design is a \emph{sharpened} likelihood
ratio, $\beta^{\ast}(t)>1$: one raises $R$ to a power above $1$, which lowers
both scalars of \Cref{thm:two} --- the \textsf{e}-power{} $c_\beta$ by
\Cref{lem:family}(i), and the exponent, since
$\Lambda(R_\beta)=\sup_{u\le1}\left\{-(1-u)\kappa(\beta)/\beta-\kappa(u)\right\}
\le\Lambda(R)$ because $\kappa(\beta)>0$ for $\beta>1$ --- and still reduces the
error, because at those horizons what matters is dispersion rather than drift.
The surrogate exponent $\lambda(\beta)$ itself turns negative there
(\Cref{lem:family}(ii)).
In the Gaussian model of \Cref{ex:gauss} at $\Delta=0.8$, $\alpha=0.05$
(crossover $\ell/D=9.4$), the optimum $\beta^{\ast}(t)=\sqrt{\ell/(tD)}$ gives
$\gamma_2=0.906$ against $0.981$ for $R$, and $\gamma_5=0.745$ against $0.782$;
the surrogate bound is vacuous at both horizons, $e^{B_2}=8.4$ and
$e^{B_5}=16.1$, yet $B_t$ ranks the two designs correctly, which is
\Cref{prp:exactfamily}(a) at work. Sharpening is not always available. If
$\ell/t\ge g(\beta_{\max}^{-})$ there is no minimiser at all and $B_t$ decreases
throughout $\mathcal{B}$; this happens at small $t$ whenever $g$ is bounded, as in
\Cref{ex:ceiling}, where $g(\infty)=\log2$ and no $\beta^{\ast}(t)$ exists for
$t\le\ell/\log2=4.3$. And if $\beta_{\max}=1$ --- $Z_\beta=\infty$ for every
$\beta>1$, as for heavy-tailed $R$ --- the family stops at $R$ and no sharpening
exists to be had. \Cref{fig:horizon} shows what the crossover is
worth in the Gaussian model.
<!-- end remark-23 -->
<!-- remark-24: body_md -->
\label{rem:bahadurrao}
\eqref{eq:capstone} is an upper bound, and one may ask by how much it errs. In
the Gaussian model of \Cref{ex:gauss} the answer is exact. There
$G_t\sim\mathcal N(tD,2tD)$ under $P_1$, so \Cref{prp:exactfamily}(a) gives
$\gamma_t(\alpha)=\Phi(-z_t)$ with
$z_t=(tD-B_t(\beta^{\ast}(t)))/\sqrt{2tD}$, and the standard normal tail
estimate $-\log\Phi(-z)=\frac{z^{2}}{2}+\log\left( z\sqrt{2\pi}\right)+o(1)$ yields
\[
   -\log\gamma_t(\alpha)\ -\ \left(-B_t(\beta^{\ast}(t))\right)
   \ =\ \tfrac12\log t\ +\ O(1)\qquad(t\to\infty) .
\]
So the bound is off by exactly half a logarithm --- the Bahadur--Rao prefactor
\cite{BR60}, \cite[\S3.7]{DZ10} --- and \eqref{eq:capstone} is tight to
$O(\log t)$. Numerically, at $\Delta=0.8$ and $\alpha=0.05$ the difference minus
$\frac12\log t$ equals $3.356$, $3.592$, $3.661$, $3.682$, $3.689$, $3.691$ at
$t=10^{2},\dots,10^{7}$, converging to the predicted
$\ell+\frac12\log(4\pi D)=3.6915$.

We expect the same to hold generally: that under the hypotheses of
\Cref{thm:betastar}(b) and a non-lattice condition on $\log R$,
\[
   -\log\gamma_t(\alpha)\ =\ t\,\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)-\sqrt{2\ell tV_0}
      +\tfrac12\log t+O(1) ,
\]
by a Bahadur--Rao expansion of $\mathbb{P}_1(G_t\le B_t(\beta))$ along the
moving threshold. We do not prove it here; the moving threshold is what makes it
more than a citation, since $B_t(\beta^{\ast}(t))-t\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)$ grows like
a fixed multiple of $t$ rather than staying at a bounded deviation.
<!-- end remark-24 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{lem:floor}
Let $E\in\mathcal{E}$ with $c:=\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[\log E]>0$ and $v:=\operatorname{Var}_{P_1}(\log E)<\infty$,
let $(W_t)_{t\in\mathbb{N}_0}$ be the i.i.d.\ product it generates, and suppose
$c\,\ell>2v$. Then
\[
   \bar\gamma_t(\alpha)\ \ge\ 1-\frac{2v}{c\,\ell}
   \qquad\text{for every }t\le\frac{\ell}{2c} .
\]
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
Write $S_n:=\log W_n=\sum_{m\le n}\log E(X_m)$ and $M_n:=S_n-nc$, so
$(M_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}_0}$ is a mean-zero random walk under $\mathbb{P}_1$ with
$\operatorname{Var}_{\mathbb{P}_1}(M_n)=nv$. Fix $t\le\ell/(2c)$. For $n\le t$ we have
$nc\le\ell/2$, so $\{S_n>\ell\}\subseteq\{M_n>\ell/2\}$ and hence
\[
   \mathbb{P}_1\left(\tau_\alpha\le t\right)
   =\mathbb{P}_1\left(\max_{n\le t}S_n>\ell\right)
   \ \le\ \mathbb{P}_1\left(\max_{n\le t}|M_n|\ge\tfrac\ell2\right)
   \ \le\ \frac{tv}{(\ell/2)^{2}}\ \le\ \frac{2v}{c\,\ell} ,
\]
by Kolmogorov's maximal inequality (\Cref{thm:app-kolmogorov},
\cite[Thm.~22.4]{Bil95}) and then $t\le\ell/(2c)$. The hypothesis $c\ell>2v$ is
what makes the conclusion non-trivial.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:price}
Assume $\operatorname{Var}_{P_1}(\log R)<\infty$ and apply \Cref{lem:floor} to $E=R_\beta$,
with $v_\beta=\beta^{2}\operatorname{Var}_{P_1}(\log R)$ and $c_\beta$ as in \eqref{eq:cbeta}.
Whenever $c_\beta\ell>2v_\beta$, the design $R_\beta$ has power at most
$2v_\beta/(c_\beta\ell)=O(\beta)$ at every horizon $t\le\ell/(2c_\beta)$, and
$\ell/(2c_\beta)\sim\ell/\left(2\beta(\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)+\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0))\right)$ diverges
like $\beta^{-1}$ as $\beta\downarrow0$.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- remark-25: body_md -->
\label{rem:price}
\Cref{cor:price} is the counterweight to \Cref{thm:ceiling}. Buying an exponent
within $\epsilon$ of the ceiling costs a tilt of order $\epsilon$
(\Cref{thm:betastar}(b)) and therefore a horizon of order $\epsilon^{-1}$
before anything happens at all. In the model of \Cref{ex:ceiling}, at
$\beta=0.1$ --- an exponent $90\%$ of the ceiling --- the floor gives
$\bar\gamma_t(0.05)\ge0.9315$ for every $t\le389$, and the Chernoff bound
$e^{B_t(\beta)}$ stays above $1$ until $t>1632$. The ceiling of
\Cref{thm:ceiling} is an asymptotic statement, and \Cref{cor:price} says how
asymptotic.
<!-- end remark-25 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
\label{ex:gauss}
Let $\mathcal{X}=\mathbb{R}$, $P_0=\mathcal N(0,1)$ and $P_1=\mathcal N(\Delta,1)$ with
$\Delta>0$, so $R(x)=e^{\Delta x-\Delta^{2}/2}$ and
$\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)=\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)=\frac{\Delta^{2}}2=:D$. Every quantity of this
paper is elementary here:
\[
   Z_\beta=e^{-\beta(1-\beta)\Delta^{2}/2},\qquad
   \lambda(\beta)=(1-\beta)\,D,\qquad
   c_\beta=\beta(2-\beta)\,D,\qquad
   V_0=\Delta^{2}=2D .
\]
Thus the fraction of the ceiling available at tilt $\beta$ is exactly $1-\beta$.
A direct computation gives moreover
\[
   \Lambda(R_\beta)=D\left(1-\tfrac\beta2\right)^{2}\ \ (0<\beta<2),
   \qquad
   \Lambda(R_\beta)=0\ \ (\beta\ge2),
   \qquad\text{so}\qquad
   \Lambda(R)=\Lambda(R_1)=\tfrac D4 :
\]
the growth-optimal \textsf{e}-variable{} realises exactly one quarter of the ceiling, its
exponent being the Chernoff information of the pair. The crossover of
\Cref{thm:betastar}(a) is at $t=\ell/D$, and for $t\ge\ell/D$ the
horizon-optimal tilt is $\beta^{\ast}(t)=\sqrt{\ell/(tD)}$ exactly, not merely
to leading order; here $g(\beta)=D\beta^{2}$, so the same formula gives
$\beta^{\ast}(t)$ at every $t$, and returns a value above $1$ for $t<\ell/D$
(\Cref{rem:sharpen}).

Here $G_t\sim\mathcal N(tD,2tD)$ under $P_1$, so \Cref{prp:exactfamily}(a)
makes the type-II error of every $R_\beta$ an explicit normal tail, with
$-\log\gamma_t(\alpha)=\frac{(tD-B_t(\beta))^{2}}{4tD}(1+o(1))$. The two rows
below record that leading term, divided by $tD$: it is $(1-\beta^{\ast}(t))^{2}$
at the horizon-optimal tilt and $\frac14(1-\frac{\ell}{tD})^{2}$ at $\beta=1$.
(The exact $-\log\gamma_t(\alpha)/(tD)$ is larger at every finite $t$ --- at
$t=50$ it is $45.7\%$ and $28.3\%$ --- because the normal tail carries a
logarithmic prefactor; the two entries below are on one basis and are the
quantities that converge to the exponents.) Numerically, at
$\Delta=0.8$ (so $D=0.32$) and $\alpha=0.05$:

\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrrrr@{}}
\toprule
horizon $t$ & $50$ & $200$ & $1\,000$ & $5\,000$ & $20\,000$\\
\midrule
$\beta^{\ast}(t)$ & $0.433$ & $0.216$ & $0.097$ & $0.043$ & $0.022$\\
$(1-\beta^{\ast}(t))^{2}$, for $R_{\beta^{\ast}(t)}$
   & $32\%$ & $61\%$ & $82\%$ & $92\%$ & $96\%$\\
$\frac14(1-\frac{\ell}{tD})^{2}$, for $R$
   & $17\%$ & $23\%$ & $24.5\%$ & $24.9\%$ & $25.0\%$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\noindent
The crossover $\ell/D=9.4$ is early here, and past it the horizon-optimal
design beats the growth-optimal one at every horizon: the exponent of $R$ tends
to a quarter of $tD$, while the exponent at $\beta^{\ast}(t)$ tends to $tD$
itself. Because $\log R$ has a density here, the improvement is strict at
every $t>\ell/D$.
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- definition-16: body_md -->
\label{def:rolling}
Fix a horizon $T\in\mathbb{N}$. For $t\le T$ put
\[
   \ell_{t-1}:=\left(\ell-\log W_{t-1}\right)_+ ,
   \qquad m_t:=T-t+1 ,
\]
the \emph{residual threshold} and the number of remaining bets, and define the
predictable tilt
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rolling}
   \beta_{t-1}\ :=\ \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\beta\in\mathcal{B}}\
   \frac1\beta\left[\frac{\ell_{t-1}}{m_t}+\kappa(\beta)\right] .
\end{equation}
The associated design bets $E_t:=R_{\beta_{t-1}}$ at step $t$.
<!-- end definition-16 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{lem:rolling}
Let $g(\beta):=\beta\kappa'(\beta)-\kappa(\beta)$ on $\mathcal{B}$. Under
the hypotheses of \Cref{thm:betastar}:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),leftmargin=2.4em]
\item $g$ is strictly increasing, with $g(0^{+})=0$ and
      $g(1)=\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)$, and, provided $\ell_{t-1}/m_t<g(\beta_{\max}^{-})$,
      the minimiser in \eqref{eq:rolling} is the unique solution of
      \begin{equation}\label{eq:rolling-root}
         g\left(\beta_{t-1}\right)\ =\ \frac{\ell_{t-1}}{m_t} ,
      \end{equation}
      while if $\ell_{t-1}/m_t\ge g(\beta_{\max}^{-})$ the infimum is approached
      as $\beta\uparrow\beta_{\max}$ and we set $\beta_{t-1}$ to the largest
      computationally admissible value;
      with the convention $\beta_{t-1}:=0$, that is $E_t:=1$, when
      $\ell_{t-1}=0$ (there the infimum is approached as $\beta\downarrow0$ and
      not attained);
\item $\beta_{t-1}$ is $\mathcal{F}_{t-1}$-measurable, so $(E_t)_{t\le T}$ is a betting
      sequence and \Cref{thm:typeI} applies unchanged;
\item $\beta_{t-1}$ is nonincreasing in $W_{t-1}$, and nondecreasing in $\ell$
      and --- at fixed $\ell_{t-1}$ --- in $t$: one bets harder when behind or
      when time runs short, and coasts once ahead;
\item $\beta_{t-1}\ge1$ if and only if
      $\ell_{t-1}/m_t\ge\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
(a) Writing the bracket as $\frac{\ell_{t-1}/m_t+\kappa(\beta)}{\beta}$, its
derivative in $\beta$ has the sign of $\beta\kappa'(\beta)-\kappa(\beta)
-\ell_{t-1}/m_t=g(\beta)-\ell_{t-1}/m_t$; and $g'(\beta)=\beta\kappa''(\beta)>0$
with $g(0^{+})=-\kappa(0^{+})=0$, $g(1)=\kappa'(1)-\kappa(1)=\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)$, as
in the proof of \Cref{lem:family}. (b) $W_{t-1}$ is $\mathcal{F}_{t-1}$-measurable and
$m_t$ is deterministic. (c) $\ell_{t-1}$ is nonincreasing in $W_{t-1}$ and nondecreasing in $\ell$,
and $m_t$ is decreasing in $t$; apply $g^{-1}$, which is increasing. (d) is
\eqref{eq:rolling-root} with $g(1)=\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)$.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- remark-26: body_md -->
\label{rem:rolling-newton}
Only \eqref{eq:rolling-root} has to be solved, and $g$ is increasing, so
bisection always works and Newton's method converges quickly from a bisection
safeguard, using
\[
   \kappa'(\beta)=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{P_0}\left[ R^{\beta}\log R\right]}{Z_\beta} ,
   \qquad
   \kappa''(\beta)=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{P_0}\left[ R^{\beta}\log^{2}R\right]}{Z_\beta}
      -\kappa'(\beta)^{2} ,
   \qquad
   g'(\beta)=\beta\,\kappa''(\beta) ,
\]
so that the Newton step is
$\beta\mapsto\beta-\left( g(\beta)-\ell_{t-1}/m_t\right)/\left(\beta\kappa''(\beta)\right)$.
When $\kappa$ is not available in closed form the three expectations are over
the \emph{known} null $P_0$, so they are a quadrature or Monte-Carlo problem and
not a statistical one; a single sample from $P_0$, drawn once and reused, gives
plug-in values at every $\beta$ and every step. In the Gaussian model of
\Cref{ex:gauss}, $g(\beta)=D\beta^{2}$ with $D=\Delta^{2}/2$ and
\eqref{eq:rolling-root} is explicit,
$\beta_{t-1}=\sqrt{\ell_{t-1}/(m_tD)}$.
<!-- end remark-26 -->
<!-- remark-27: body_md -->
\label{rem:rolling-numbers}
\Cref{def:rolling} minimises a \emph{bound} on the residual error, not the error
itself, so it is a heuristic and not an optimum: the exactly optimal predictable
rule is the value function of a finite-horizon control problem with state
$(t,\log W_{t-1})$, which has no closed form. Numerically it recovers almost all
of what that control problem achieves. In the Gaussian model of
\Cref{ex:gauss} with $\Delta=1$ and $\alpha=0.05$, computed on a grid:
\begin{center}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrr@{}}
\toprule
horizon $T$ & $20$ & $50$ & $100$\\
\midrule
best constant $\beta$, from \Cref{thm:betastar}
   & $2.15\cdot10^{-2}$ & $1.89\cdot10^{-6}$ & $2.14\cdot10^{-14}$\\
rolling-horizon tilt \eqref{eq:rolling}
   & $7.12\cdot10^{-3}$ & $1.53\cdot10^{-7}$ & $3.61\cdot10^{-16}$\\
optimal predictable rule
   & $6.46\cdot10^{-3}$ & $1.10\cdot10^{-7}$ & $1.67\cdot10^{-16}$\\
\midrule
\multicolumn{4}{@{}l@{}}{\footnotesize all three restricted to
   $\beta\in(0,1]$; \Cref{rem:rolling-beyond1} lifts the cap}\\
\midrule
share of the attainable gain & $95.6\%$ & $97.6\%$ & $99.1\%$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
<!-- end remark-27 -->
<!-- remark-28: body_md -->
\label{rem:rolling-beyond1}
By \Cref{lem:rolling}(d) the rule takes $\beta_{t-1}>1$ exactly when the
residual gap per remaining bet exceeds the largest attainable \textsf{e}-power{}. This is
the predictable counterpart of \Cref{rem:sharpen}, and it is strictly stronger:
a constant $\beta>1$ helps only below the crossover, whereas the rule reaches
for one at any horizon once the wealth has fallen far enough behind. In the
model of \Cref{rem:rolling-numbers}, capping \eqref{eq:rolling} at $\beta=1$
multiplies the error by a factor $1.10$ to $1.11$ at every horizon computed
($T=5,10,20,50$), and the optimal predictable rule uses $\beta>1$ as well ---
at $T=20$ it improves from $6.46\cdot10^{-3}$ to $5.93\cdot10^{-3}$ once
$\beta\le2$ is allowed. The reason is that the increment of $\log W$ under
$\mathbb{P}_1$ has mean $c_\beta$, concave in $\beta$ and decreasing past $\beta=1$
(\Cref{lem:family}(i)), while its standard deviation stays exactly proportional
to $\beta$; so raising $\beta$ past $1$ buys dispersion at the cost of drift ---
which is what a design that is behind with few bets left should want. It is the
same point as \Cref{thm:nfl}, in the opposite direction: a design can be
improved by lowering its \textsf{e}-power{}.
<!-- end remark-28 -->
<!-- remark-29: body_md -->
\label{rem:rolling-limits}
Three limitations. The rule is horizon-specific: $T$ is fixed in advance and the
target is $\gamma_T$; for $\bar\gamma_T$ the residual problem acquires an
absorbing region above the threshold and \eqref{eq:rolling} is no longer the
right surrogate. The exact identity of \Cref{prp:exactfamily} is lost, since
$\log W_t=\beta G_t-t\kappa(\beta)$ requires one common $\beta$; the error must
be evaluated numerically. And the \emph{certified} exponent does not improve:
\Cref{cor:ceiling} binds every betting sequence, so no predictable choice of
$\beta_{t-1}$ can raise $\Lambda^{(t)}$ above the ceiling. The gain is in the
constant, not in the rate.
<!-- end remark-29 -->
<!-- remark-30: body_md -->
\label{rem:oracle}
Both hypotheses are simple and both laws are known throughout. This matters for
reading \Cref{thm:ceiling} and \Cref{thm:betastar}: the ceiling
$\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$ is an oracle quantity, and the designs that approach it,
$R_\beta=R^{\beta}/Z_\beta$, are built from $R=\frac{dP_1}{dP_0}$ and so require
$P_1$. Not needing $P_1$ is precisely the motivation for growth-rate-optimal
\textsf{e}-variables{} in a composite alternative \cite{GHK24,LRR25}. \Cref{thm:two} is a
statement about a simple alternative and does not by itself settle what happens
there; what it does show is that, already for a simple alternative, the scalar
those constructions maximise is not the one that governs the type-II error. What the composite analogue of \Cref{thm:betastar} looks like ---
how much of $\inf_{P_1\in\mathcal{H}_1}\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$ is available to a design that does
not know which $P_1$ obtains --- is not addressed here.
<!-- end remark-30 -->
<!-- remark-31: body_md -->
\label{rem:eproc}
\Cref{def:wealth} builds $(W_t)_{t\in\mathbb{N}_0}$ as a product of conditional
\textsf{e}-variables{}. Some of the results extend beyond that class and some do not.
\Cref{prp:stein-ceiling} uses only that rejecting when $\tau_\alpha\le t$ is a
level-$\alpha$ test, so it holds for any nonnegative $\mathbb{P}_0$-supermartingale
and indeed for any \textsf{e}-process{} --- a nonnegative process dominated by a
supermartingale under every null, in the sense of
\cite{RRLK23,RGVS23}. \Cref{prp:upper-seq}\ref{it:agg-exact}--\ref{it:agg-det}
extend in a different direction --- they need no product structure at all, only
a filtration (\Cref{rem:whatgeneralises}) --- while the equality analysis of
\Cref{prp:upper-seq}\ref{it:agg-iid} does use it, through the sections
$E_n^{y}$ of \eqref{eq:fubini}.
<!-- end remark-31 -->
<!-- remark-32: body_md -->
\label{rem:sprt}
\Cref{prp:exactfamily} says that the flattened family performs one
likelihood-ratio test at a moving threshold, which places \Cref{sec:horizon}
squarely in the territory of Wald's sequential probability ratio test
\cite{Wal45}: there too the statistic is $G_t$, there too the two error
probabilities are governed by $\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)$ and $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$ in opposite
roles, and there too the asymmetry between the two divergences is the source of
the design trade-off. What is different here is the constraint. The SPRT
chooses two thresholds and stops between them; a test supermartingale{} is constrained to have
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[W_t\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}]\le W_{t-1}$, which buys type-I validity at every
stopping time simultaneously and fixes the upper threshold at $\frac1\alpha$.
\Cref{thm:ceiling} is the price of that constraint, and \Cref{thm:betastar} says
what remains free once it is imposed.

A second point of contact is with how the safe-testing literature sizes
experiments. Sample-size rules there are typically driven by the \textsf{e}-power{}, via
$t\approx\ell/\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[\log E]$ --- which \Cref{prp:exactfamily}(c) shows is
exactly the horizon at which the threshold $B_t(\beta)$ crosses the mean of
$G_t$, so the heuristic is locating the right horizon for the wrong reason.
\Cref{thm:nfl} says the heuristic cannot be turned into a guarantee uniform over
testing problems, and \Cref{lem:floor} says what a variance hypothesis buys
instead.
<!-- end remark-32 -->
<!-- remark-33: body_md -->
\label{rem:scopefinal}
The finite-horizon content of this paper is \eqref{eq:matched-error},
\Cref{prp:exactfamily} and \Cref{cor:price}; \Cref{thm:ceiling} itself is a
statement about an exponent, and the rate at which that exponent is approached
is quantified only to the order of the second term. The exact second-order
behaviour --- the constant in the $O(1)$ of \eqref{eq:capstone}, the
Bahadur--Rao prefactor \cite{BR60}, and the matching converse --- is not
treated here.
Nor is misspecification. The upper bounds \Cref{thm:upper} and
\Cref{prp:upper-seq} hold for an arbitrary \textsf{e}-variable{}, so they are untouched by
it; what a misspecified $R$ costs is the \emph{attainment} half, since the
designs $R_\beta$ are built from the true likelihood ratio.

Nor, in the general filtered setting, is the ceiling known to be sharp. The
upper bound \Cref{cor:ceiling} holds there with no structural hypothesis at all,
and \Cref{lem:flat-cond} supplies a witness step by step; what is missing is a
reason for the per-step values to aggregate, and \Cref{ass:homog} --- that the
conditional divergences be non-random --- is a sufficient condition rather than
a characterisation. Whether the essential suprema in \eqref{eq:ceiling} can be
strict is open, as is the exponent of the sequential error, for which
\Cref{prp:exponent} claims only a $\liminf$.

Finally, this paper says what the exponent \emph{can} be, not what a given
design can be \emph{certified} to achieve. The two questions are independent,
and the second is the subject of the companion paper \cite{LADDER}, which
converts hypotheses on the lower tail of $\log E_n$ into explicit
finite-horizon bounds, under an arbitrary filtration and with no product
structure. Composite hypotheses, which \Cref{rem:oracle} leaves open here, are
treated there.
<!-- end remark-33 -->
<!-- definition-17: body_md -->
\label{def:kl-cond}
For $t\in\mathbb{N}$ put
$\mathrm{KL}_t:=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}\left[\log R_t\mid\mathcal{F}_{t-1}\right]\in[0,\infty]$.
By the chain rule and \Cref{ass:standing},
$\sum_{n\le t}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[\mathrm{KL}_n]=\mathrm{KL}(\mathbb{P}_1|_{\mathcal{F}_t}\|\mathbb{P}_0|_{\mathcal{F}_t})<\infty$,
so $\mathrm{KL}_t<\infty$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s. In the i.i.d.\ model $\mathrm{KL}_t=\mathrm{KL}(P_1\|P_0)$
$\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.
<!-- end definition-17 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{lem:epower-cond}
Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a betting sequence and $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Then $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.
\[
   \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}\left[(\log E_n)_+\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}\right]\ \le\ \mathrm{KL}_n+1 ,
   \qquad
   \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}\left[\log E_n\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}\right]\ \le\ \mathrm{KL}_n ,
\]
with equality in the second bound if and only if $E_n=R_n$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
By \Cref{lem:supmg}, $E_n<\infty$ $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s., so $(\log E_n)_+\in\mathbb{R}$ on a
$\mathbb{P}_0$-full set. Young's inequality $xy\le x\log x-x+e^{y}$ ($x\ge0$,
$y\in\mathbb{R}$) applied there at $x=R_n$, $y=(\log E_n)_+$, under $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[\,\cdot\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]$ and with
\Cref{lem:bayes}, gives
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[(\log E_n)_+\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]\le(\mathrm{KL}_n-1)+
\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[\max(1,E_n)\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]\le\mathrm{KL}_n+1$, using
$\max(1,E_n)\le1+E_n$ and \Cref{def:cond-evar}. For the second bound,
$R_n>0$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.\ by \Cref{lem:bayes}, and conditional Jensen for the
concave $\log$ gives
\[
   \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}\left[\log\tfrac{E_n}{R_n}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}\right]
   \ \le\ \log\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}\left[\tfrac{E_n}{R_n}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}\right]
   \ =\ \log\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}\left[ E_n\mathbf 1_{\{R_n>0\}}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}\right]
   \ \le\ 0 .
\]
Equality forces, by strict concavity, $E_n/R_n$ to be $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.\ equal to an
$\mathcal{F}_{n-1}$-measurable $\varkappa$, and then
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[E_n\mathbf 1_{\{R_n>0\}}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]=1$ gives
$\varkappa\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[R_n\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]=\varkappa=1$.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{lem:limit-cond}
For every $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s.,
\[
   \lambda_n(0^{+})\ =\ \overline{\mathrm{KL}}_n\ :=\ -\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}\left[\log R_n\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}\right]
   \ \in[0,\infty] ,
\]
the conditional relative entropy of $\mathbb{P}_0$ with respect to $\mathbb{P}_1$ over
step $n$. In the i.i.d.\ model $\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_n=\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
Put $h_\beta:=\frac{R_n^{\beta}-1}{\beta}$ for $\beta\in(0,1]$. For fixed
$x\in[0,\infty)$ the map $\beta\mapsto\frac{x^{\beta}-1}{\beta}$ is
nondecreasing on $(0,1]$ and decreases to $\log x$ as $\beta\downarrow0$ (for
$x>0$ it is a difference quotient of the convex $\beta\mapsto e^{\beta\log x}$;
for $x=0$ it is $-\frac1\beta$). Hence $h_\beta\downarrow\log R_n$ pointwise,
with $h_\beta\le h_1=R_n-1$ and
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[|R_n-1|\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]\le2$ by \Cref{lem:Zf-cond}(i). Conditional
monotone convergence for the decreasing family $(h_\beta)$ dominated above by an
integrable variable gives
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[h_\beta\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]\to\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[\log R_n\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]
=-\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_n$ $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s.; the conditional expectation is well defined in
$[-\infty,0]$ because $(\log R_n)_+\le R_n$.

Now $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[h_\beta\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]=\frac{Z_{\beta,n}-1}{\beta}$ and
$\lambda_n(\beta)=-\frac{\log Z_{\beta,n}}{\beta}$. Both events below are
$\mathcal{F}_{n-1}$-measurable. On $\left\{\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_n<\infty\right\}$ we get $Z_{\beta,n}\to1$, so
$\log Z_{\beta,n}=(Z_{\beta,n}-1)(1+o(1))$ and
$\lambda_n(\beta)\to\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_n$. On $\left\{\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_n=\infty\right\}$ we get
$\frac{Z_{\beta,n}-1}{\beta}\to-\infty$, and $\log y\le y-1$ for $y>0$ gives
$\lambda_n(\beta)\ge-\frac{Z_{\beta,n}-1}{\beta}\to\infty$.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- definition-18: body_md -->
\label{def:flat-cond}
For $\beta\in(0,1]$ and $n\in\mathbb{N}$ put
$R_{\beta,n}:=R_n^{\beta}/Z_{\beta,n}$ on $\left\{0<Z_{\beta,n}<\infty\right\}$ and
$R_{\beta,n}:=1$ elsewhere. In the i.i.d.\ model $R_{\beta,n}=R_\beta(X_n)$
$\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.
<!-- end definition-18 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{lem:flat-cond}
For every $\beta\in(0,1]$ and $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $R_{\beta,n}$ is a conditional \textsf{e}-variable{}
at time $n$, and with $s=\frac{1-\beta}{\beta}$,
\[
   \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}\left[ R_{\beta,n}^{-s}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}\right]\ =\ e^{-\lambda_n(\beta)}
   \qquad\mathbb{P}_1\text{-a.s.}
\]
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[R_{\beta,n}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]=Z_{\beta,n}^{-1}
\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[R_n^{\beta}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]=1$ $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s.\ by
\Cref{lem:Zf-cond}(i) and \Cref{rem:Zf-cond}, so $R_{\beta,n}$ is a conditional
\textsf{e}-variable{} in the sense of \Cref{def:cond-evar}. Since $\beta s=1-\beta$, we have $1-\beta s=\beta$, so
\Cref{lem:bayes} gives
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[R_n^{-\beta s}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]
=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[R_n^{1-\beta s}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]=Z_{\beta,n}$, whence
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[R_{\beta,n}^{-s}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]
=Z_{\beta,n}^{s}\,Z_{\beta,n}=Z_{\beta,n}^{1/\beta}=e^{-\lambda_n(\beta)}$.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prp:equality-cond}
Let $s\in(0,\infty)$, $\beta=\frac1{1+s}$, $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Then
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[E_n^{-s}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]=e^{-\lambda_n(\beta)}$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.\ if
and only if $E_n=R_{\beta,n}$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s. Consequently equality holds in
\Cref{prp:upper-seq}\ref{it:agg-exact} for a given $t$ if and only if
$E_n=R_{\beta,n}$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.\ for every $n\le t$.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
Sufficiency is \Cref{lem:flat-cond}. For necessity, equality forces equality in
both steps of the proof of \Cref{thm:upper-cond}. Under the equality hypothesis
$A^{r}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[E_n\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]\in(0,1]$ and
$B^{r'}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[E_n^{-s}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]=e^{-\lambda_n(\beta)}\in(0,1]$
$\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.\ by \Cref{lem:Zf-cond}(i), so the proviso of the equality clause
of \Cref{cor:app-holder} holds and that clause gives
$G^{r}/A^{r}=H^{r'}/B^{r'}$ $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s.; with $G=E_n^{1-\beta}$,
$r=\frac1{1-\beta}$, $H=(R_nE_n^{-s})^{\beta}$, $r'=\frac1\beta$ this reads
$E_n^{1+s}=\varkappa'R_n$ $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s.\ with $\varkappa'$
$\mathcal{F}_{n-1}$-measurable, hence $E_n=\varkappa R_n^{\beta}$ $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s.\ with
$\varkappa:=(\varkappa')^{\beta}$. Equality in the constraint step requires
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[E_n\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]=1$, that is $\varkappa Z_{\beta,n}=1$. For the last claim, the induction proving
\Cref{prp:upper-seq}\ref{it:agg-exact} runs through equalities if and only if
each of its steps does, and $M_{n-1}\in(0,\infty)$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:chernoffinfo-cond}
Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and assume $\mathbb{P}_0(R_n>0\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1})=1$ $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s.\ --- the
conditional form of $P_0\ll P_1$, and implied by $\lambda_n(0^{+})<\infty$
(\Cref{lem:limit-cond}) but not conversely. Then
\[
   \sup_{s\ge0}\left\{-\log\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}\left[ R_n^{-s}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}\right]\right\}
   \ =\ \sup_{\beta\in(0,1]}\beta\,\lambda_n(\beta)
   \qquad\mathbb{P}_1\text{-a.s.},
\]
the conditional Chernoff information of the one-step kernels. Without the
hypothesis the left-hand side may be $+\infty$ while the right-hand side is
finite.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
Since $R_n>0$ $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s.\ conditionally, \Cref{lem:bayes} gives
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[R_n^{-s}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[R_n^{1-s}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]
=Z_{1-s,n}$ for \emph{every} $s\ge0$, so the left-hand side is
$\sup_{\beta\le1}\left\{-\log Z_{\beta,n}\right\}$ under $\beta=1-s$. By
\Cref{rem:Zf-cond} the map $\beta\mapsto\log Z_{\beta,n}$ is convex and vanishes
at $\beta=0$ and $\beta=1$, hence is $\ge0$ on $\beta\le0$; so the supremum is
attained on $\beta\in(0,1]$, where $-\log Z_{\beta,n}=\beta\lambda_n(\beta)$.
For the last sentence take $P_0=\mathrm{Bern}(\frac12)$, $P_1=\delta_1$ of
\Cref{rem:eqcase}: then $\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[R^{-s}]=2^{-s}$ for every $s\ge0$, so the left
side is $+\infty$, while $\sup_\beta\beta\lambda(\beta)=\log2$.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- assumption-2: body_md -->
\label{ass:homog}
For every $\beta\in(0,1]$ and every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ there is a constant
$z_n(\beta)\in(0,1]$ with $Z_{\beta,n}=z_n(\beta)$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.; equivalently,
$\lambda_n(\beta)$ is $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.\ constant. No constancy in $n$ is required.
It suffices to require this for rational $\beta$: if $\beta_k\to\beta$ then
$R_n^{\beta_k}\to R_n^{\beta}$ pointwise, dominated by $1+R_n$, so conditional
dominated convergence gives $Z_{\beta_k,n}\to Z_{\beta,n}$ $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s. Also
$\lambda_n(0^{+})=\sup_{\beta}\lambda_n(\beta)$ is then $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.\
constant. The qualifier must be $\mathbb{P}_1$ and not $\mathbb{P}_0$: on
$\left\{ L_{n-1}=0\right\}$, which \Cref{def:ratios} may charge under $\mathbb{P}_0$, the
convention $R_n:=1$ makes $Z_{\beta,n}=1$, so even in the i.i.d.\ model
$Z_{\beta,n}$ is $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s.\ constant only when $P_0\sim P_1$. Every use
below sits inside a $\mathbb{P}_1$-expectation or an $\operatorname{ess\,sup}$ under
$\mathbb{P}_1$.
<!-- end assumption-2 -->
<!-- remark-34: body_md -->
\label{rem:homog}
\Cref{ass:homog} holds whenever $\mathbb{P}_0,\mathbb{P}_1$ are product measures with
$\mathcal{F}_t$ generated by the coordinates --- the observations independent, not
necessarily identically distributed --- since then $R_n$ agrees $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.\
with a function of the $n$-th coordinate alone and
$Z_{\beta,n}=\mathbb{E}_{P_{0,n}}[R_n^{\beta}]$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s. In particular it holds
for \Cref{con:nfl}, and in the i.i.d.\ model with $z_n(\beta)=Z_\beta$. It fails as soon as the one-step conditional R\'enyi
divergences depend on the past.
<!-- end remark-34 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{lem:family-cond}
For $\beta\in(0,1]$ and $n\in\mathbb{N}$ put
$c_{\beta,n}:=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[\log R_{\beta,n}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]$. Then $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cbeta-cond}
   c_{\beta,n}\ =\ \beta\left(\mathrm{KL}_n+\lambda_n(\beta)\right) ,
\end{equation}
with $\mathrm{KL}_n$ as in \Cref{def:kl-cond}. Call $R_n$ \emph{conditionally
non-degenerate} on an event $B\in\mathcal{F}_{n-1}$ if there is no
$\mathcal{F}_{n-1}$-measurable $V$ with $R_n=V$ $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s.\ on $B$. If moreover
$\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_n<\infty$ and $R_n$ is conditionally non-degenerate, then
$\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.\ $\beta\mapsto c_{\beta,n}$ is strictly increasing on $(0,1)$
with $c_{0^{+},n}=0$ and $c_{1,n}=\mathrm{KL}_n$; $\beta\mapsto\lambda_n(\beta)$ is
strictly decreasing with $\lambda_n(0^{+})=\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_n$ and $\lambda_n(1)=0$; and
$c_{\beta,n}/\beta\uparrow\mathrm{KL}_n+\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_n$ as $\beta\downarrow0$.
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
$\log R_{\beta,n}=\beta\log R_n-\kappa_n(\beta)$ with
$\kappa_n(\beta):=\log Z_{\beta,n}=-\beta\lambda_n(\beta)$; take
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[\,\cdot\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]$ and use \Cref{def:kl-cond} for
\eqref{eq:cbeta-cond}. For the rest, the proof of \Cref{lem:family} applies to
$\kappa_n$ with three substitutions: $\mathbb{E}_{P_0}$ by
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[\,\cdot\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]$, monotone and dominated convergence by
their conditional forms, and \Cref{lem:limit} by \Cref{lem:limit-cond}. Four
inputs are needed, and all are available.
$\kappa_n(1)=0$ by \Cref{lem:Zf-cond}(i).
$\kappa_n(0^{+})=0$: $\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_n<\infty$ forces $\mathbb{P}_0(R_n>0\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1})=1$
(\Cref{lem:limit-cond}), and $R_n^{\beta}\to\mathbf 1_{\{R_n>0\}}$ dominated by
$1+R_n$ gives $Z_{\beta,n}\to1$.
$\kappa_n'(1)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[R_n\log R_n\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]=\mathrm{KL}_n<\infty$
$\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.\ by \Cref{lem:bayes} and \Cref{def:kl-cond}; the interchange at
$\beta\uparrow1$ is conditional monotone convergence on $\left\{ R_n\ge1\right\}$ and
conditional dominated convergence on $\left\{ R_n<1\right\}$, where
$R_n^{\beta}|\log R_n|\le\frac1{e\beta_0}$ for $\beta\ge\beta_0>0$.
Finally $\kappa_n$ is \emph{strictly} convex where $R_n$ is conditionally
non-degenerate: for $\beta_1\ne\beta_2$ and $\rho\in(0,1)$, conditional
H\"older gives
$\kappa_n(\rho\beta_1+(1-\rho)\beta_2)\le\rho\kappa_n(\beta_1)
+(1-\rho)\kappa_n(\beta_2)$, and by the equality clause of
\Cref{cor:app-holder} equality forces $R_n^{\beta_1-\beta_2}$ to equal an
$\mathcal{F}_{n-1}$-measurable variable $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s., hence $R_n$ to do so. This
replaces the tilted-measure argument of \Cref{lem:family} and needs no regular
conditional distribution.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:ceiling-gen}
Under \Cref{ass:homog}, let $\mathcal W$ be the class of all betting sequences.
For every $t\in\mathbb{N}$,
\[
   \sup_{\mathcal W}\ \Lambda^{(t)}
   \ =\ \frac1t\sum_{n\le t}\lambda_n(0^{+})
   \ =\ \frac1t\sum_{n\le t}\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_n
\]
(the second equality by \Cref{lem:limit-cond}, the right-hand side denoting the
$\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.\ constant value of $\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_n$),
approached along $(R_{\beta,n})_{n\le t}$ as $\beta\downarrow0$; and
$\Lambda^{(t)}_s=\frac1t\sum_{n\le t}\lambda_n(\beta)$ for the betting sequence
$E_n=R_{\beta,n}$, $\beta=\frac1{1+s}$. If moreover $\lambda_n(0^{+})<\infty$ for every $n\le t$, $R_n$ is conditionally non-degenerate in the
sense of \Cref{lem:family-cond} for some $n\le t$, and the betting sequence in question
has $\mathbb{P}_0(W_t\ne1)>0$, then the supremum is not attained by it.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
$\le$: \Cref{cor:ceiling}, whose essential suprema are here the constants
$\lambda_n(0^{+})$ of \Cref{ass:homog}. $\ge$: for $E_n=R_{\beta,n}$, \Cref{lem:flat-cond} and
the tower property give
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[W_n^{-s}]=e^{-\lambda_n(\beta)}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[W_{n-1}^{-s}]$,
because $\lambda_n(\beta)$ is a constant; hence
$\Lambda^{(t)}_s=\frac1t\sum_{n\le t}\lambda_n(\beta)$. Each
$\lambda_n(\cdot)$ is nonincreasing (\Cref{lem:Zf-cond}(ii)), so the finite sum
is nonincreasing in $\beta$ and its supremum over $\beta\in(0,1]$ is
$\frac1t\sum_{n\le t}\lambda_n(0^{+})$ by monotone convergence. Taking the
supremum over $s\ge0$ and over $\mathcal W$ in either order gives the
displayed identity.

For non-attainment, suppose $\Lambda^{(t)}=\frac1t\sum_{n\le t}\lambda_n(0^{+})$
for some betting sequence with $\mathbb{P}_0(W_t\ne1)>0$. First,
$\lambda_n(0^{+})<\infty$ forces $\mathbb{P}_0(R_n>0\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1})=1$
(\Cref{cor:chernoffinfo-cond}), so by induction $\mathbb{P}_0(L_t>0)=1$ and therefore
$\mathbb{P}_0|_{\mathcal{F}_t}\sim\mathbb{P}_1|_{\mathcal{F}_t}$. \Cref{lem:attained} --- whose proof uses
only that equivalence and $\mathbb{P}_0(W_t\ne1)>0$ --- then supplies an
$s^{\ast}\in[0,\infty)$ with $\Lambda^{(t)}=\Lambda^{(t)}_{s^{\ast}}$, and
$s^{\ast}>0$ because $\Lambda^{(t)}_0=0$ while the right-hand side is positive
(strict conditional Jensen below). Hence
$\lambda_n(\beta^{\ast})=\lambda_n(0^{+})$ for every $n\le t$ with
$\beta^{\ast}=\frac1{1+s^{\ast}}$; by \Cref{lem:Zf-cond}(ii) this forces
$\lambda_n$ to be constant on $(0,\beta^{\ast}]$. But $\lambda_n(\beta)$ is
minus the slope of the chord of $\kappa_n$ from $0$ to $\beta$, and
$\kappa_n(0^{+})=0$ with $\kappa_n$ strictly convex
(\Cref{lem:family-cond}, using $\lambda_n(0^{+})<\infty$ and conditional
non-degeneracy) makes that slope strictly increasing, so $\lambda_n$ is
strictly decreasing --- a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prp:exactfamily-gen}
Under \Cref{ass:homog}, fix $\beta\in(0,1]$ and let $(W_t)_{t\in\mathbb{N}_0}$ be
generated by $E_n=R_{\beta,n}$. Put $G_t:=\log L_t$ and
$B_t(\beta):=\frac1\beta\left(\ell+\sum_{n\le t}\log z_n(\beta)\right)$. Then
$\log W_t=\beta\left( G_t-B_t(\beta)\right)+\ell$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s., and
\[
   \gamma_t(\alpha)=\mathbb{P}_1\left( G_t\le B_t(\beta)\right) ,
   \qquad
   \bar\gamma_t(\alpha)=\mathbb{P}_1\left( G_n\le B_n(\beta)\ \text{for all }n\le t\right) .
\]
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
$\log R_{\beta,n}=\beta\log R_n-\log z_n(\beta)$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s., and
$\sum_{n\le t}\log R_n=\log L_t$; sum and rearrange. Then
$\log W_t\le\ell$ is $G_t\le B_t(\beta)$, and applying this at every $n\le t$
gives the second identity, by \Cref{def:typeII}.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- remark-35: body_md -->
\label{rem:betastar-gen}
On $\beta\in(0,1]$, \Cref{thm:betastar} carries over verbatim, with
$\lambda(\beta)$ replaced by $\lambda_1(\beta)$, whenever \Cref{ass:homog} holds
\emph{and}
$\lambda_n(\beta)=\lambda_1(\beta)$ for every $n$: only then is
$B_t(\beta)=\frac1\beta(\ell-t\beta\lambda_1(\beta))$ affine in $t$, which is
what the analysis of $\beta\mapsto B_t(\beta)$ uses. Without constancy in $n$,
$B_t$ is still deterministic and \Cref{prp:exactfamily-gen} still reduces the
design problem to one scalar per horizon, but the crossover statement
\Cref{thm:betastar}(a) and the rate \Cref{thm:betastar}(b) have no closed form.
The extension to $\beta>1$ needs more still: every statement of
\Cref{app:general} is written for $\beta\in(0,1]$, and beyond it one would have
to require $Z_{\beta,n}$ to be finite and $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.\ constant there too,
which \Cref{ass:homog} does not provide.
<!-- end remark-35 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label{lem:surrogate-gen}
Under \Cref{ass:homog}, for every $\beta\in(0,1]$, $\alpha\in(0,1)$ and
$t\in\mathbb{N}$, the betting sequence $E_n=R_{\beta,n}$ satisfies
$\gamma_t(\alpha)\le e^{B_t(\beta)}$ with
$B_t(\beta)=\frac{\ell}{\beta}-\sum_{n\le t}\lambda_n(\beta)$, in agreement with
\Cref{prp:exactfamily-gen}.
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
$R_{\beta,n}^{-1/\beta}=Z_{\beta,n}^{1/\beta}R_n^{-1}$, and
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[R_n^{-1}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]
=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[R_n R_n^{-1}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]
=\mathbb{P}_0(R_n>0\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1})\le1$ by \Cref{lem:bayes}, so
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[R_{\beta,n}^{-1/\beta}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]\le Z_{\beta,n}^{1/\beta}
=e^{-\lambda_n(\beta)}$. Since the $\lambda_n(\beta)$ are constants, the tower
induction of \Cref{prp:upper-seq}\ref{it:agg-exact} run with $\le$ in place of
$\ge$ gives
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[W_t^{-1/\beta}]\le\exp(-\sum_{n\le t}\lambda_n(\beta))$;
\Cref{lem:chernoff} at $s=\frac1\beta$ then gives the claim.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
\label{lem:doob-gen}
Let $(M_n)_{n\le t}$ be a $\mathbb{P}_1$-martingale with $M_0=0$ and
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[M_t^{2}]<\infty$. Then
$\mathbb{P}_1(\max_{n\le t}|M_n|\ge x)\le\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[M_t^{2}]/x^{2}$ for every
$x>0$.
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
Let $\sigma:=\inf\left\{ n\le t\;\middle|\;|M_n|\ge x\right\}$ and $A_n:=\left\{\sigma=n\right\}\in\mathcal{F}_n$.
Conditional Jensen gives $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[M_t^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_n]\ge M_n^{2}$, so
\[
   \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}\left[ M_t^{2}\right]\ \ge\ \sum_{n\le t}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}\left[ M_t^{2}\mathbf 1_{A_n}\right]
   \ \ge\ \sum_{n\le t}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}\left[ M_n^{2}\mathbf 1_{A_n}\right]
   \ \ge\ x^{2}\,\mathbb{P}_1(\sigma\le t) . \qedhere
\]
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- lemma-26: body_md -->
\label{lem:floor-gen}
Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a betting sequence with
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[\log E_n\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]\le c$ and
$\operatorname{Var}_{\mathbb{P}_1}(\log E_n\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1})\le v<\infty$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.\ for every
$n$, where $c>0$ and $c\,\ell>2v$. Then
$\bar\gamma_t(\alpha)\ge1-\frac{2v}{c\,\ell}$ for every $t\le\frac{\ell}{2c}$.
<!-- end lemma-26 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
Put $S_n:=\log W_n$ and
$M_n:=S_n-\sum_{m\le n}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[\log E_m\mid\mathcal{F}_{m-1}]$, a $\mathbb{P}_1$-martingale
with $M_0=0$ and orthogonal increments, so
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[M_t^{2}]=\sum_{m\le t}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[(\Delta M_m)^{2}]\le tv$. Fix
$t\le\ell/(2c)$. For $n\le t$ the drift term is at most $nc\le\ell/2$, so
$\left\{ S_n>\ell\right\}\subseteq\left\{ M_n>\frac\ell2\right\}$ and, by \Cref{lem:doob-gen},
\[
   \mathbb{P}_1(\tau_\alpha\le t)=\mathbb{P}_1\left(\max_{n\le t}S_n>\ell\right)
   \ \le\ \mathbb{P}_1\left(\max_{n\le t}|M_n|\ge\tfrac\ell2\right)
   \ \le\ \frac{tv}{(\ell/2)^{2}}\ \le\ \frac{2v}{c\,\ell} . \qedhere
\]
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:price-gen}
Assume \Cref{ass:homog}, $\operatorname{Var}_{\mathbb{P}_1}(\log R_n\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1})\le\bar v<\infty$
$\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.\ for every $n$, and
$J:=\sup_n\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{\mathbb{P}_1}\left(\mathrm{KL}_n+\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_n\right)<\infty$ --- the
last of which is what makes the horizon range below non-empty, and does not
follow from the others. Put
$\bar c_\beta:=\sup_n\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{\mathbb{P}_1}c_{\beta,n}\le\beta J$.
Then $\operatorname{Var}_{\mathbb{P}_1}(\log R_{\beta,n}\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1})\le\beta^{2}\bar v$, and
whenever $\bar c_\beta\ell>2\beta^{2}\bar v$ the design $E_n=R_{\beta,n}$ has
power at most $2\beta^{2}\bar v/(\bar c_\beta\ell)=O(\beta)$ at every horizon
$t\le\ell/(2\bar c_\beta)$, and $\ell/(2\bar c_\beta)\ge\ell/(2\beta J)$
diverges like $\beta^{-1}$ as $\beta\downarrow0$.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
$\log R_{\beta,n}=\beta\log R_n-\kappa_n(\beta)$ with $\kappa_n(\beta)$
constant, so the conditional variance scales by $\beta^{2}$; apply
\Cref{lem:floor-gen} with $c=\bar c_\beta$ and $v=\beta^{2}\bar v$. By
\eqref{eq:cbeta-cond} and $\lambda_n(\beta)\le\lambda_n(0^{+})=\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_n$,
$\bar c_\beta=\beta\sup_n\operatorname*{ess\,sup}(\mathrm{KL}_n+\lambda_n(\beta))
\le\beta J$.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- assumption-3: body_md -->
\label{ass:spectrum}
There is $D\in[0,\infty)$ such that for every $\epsilon>0$,
\[
   \mathbb{P}_0\left(-\tfrac1t\log L_t\ >\ D+\epsilon\right)\ \xrightarrow[t\to\infty]{}\ 0 .
\]
<!-- end assumption-3 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prp:stein-gen}
Under \Cref{ass:spectrum}, for every betting sequence and every
$\alpha\in(0,1)$,
\[
   \limsup_{t\to\infty}\ -\frac1t\log\bar\gamma_t(\alpha)\ \le\ D ,
\]
and the same holds with $\gamma_t(\alpha)$ in place of $\bar\gamma_t(\alpha)$.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
Fix $\epsilon>0$, put $A_t:=\{\tau_\alpha>t\}\in\mathcal{F}_t$ and
$B_t:=\left\{ L_t\ge e^{-t(D+\epsilon)}\right\}$, so $\mathbb{P}_0(B_t^{c})\to0$ by
\Cref{ass:spectrum} and $\mathbb{P}_0(A_t^{c})\le\mathbb{P}_0(\tau_\alpha<\infty)\le\alpha$
by \Cref{thm:typeI}. Since $\mathbb{P}_1\ll\mathbb{P}_0$ on $\mathcal{F}_t$ with density $L_t$,
\[
   \bar\gamma_t(\alpha)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}\left[ L_t\mathbf 1_{A_t}\right]
   \ \ge\ e^{-t(D+\epsilon)}\,\mathbb{P}_0(A_t\cap B_t)
   \ \ge\ e^{-t(D+\epsilon)}\left(1-\alpha-\mathbb{P}_0(B_t^{c})\right) .
\]
Hence $-\frac1t\log\bar\gamma_t(\alpha)\le D+\epsilon-\frac1t\log(1-\alpha-o(1))$,
and $\epsilon>0$ was arbitrary. For $\gamma_t(\alpha)$ replace $A_t$ by
$\left\{ W_t\le\frac1\alpha\right\}$, whose complement has
$\mathbb{P}_0(W_t>\frac1\alpha)\le\alpha\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[W_t]\le\alpha$ by Markov and
\Cref{lem:supmg}.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- remark-36: body_md -->
\label{rem:stein-iid}
In the i.i.d.\ model with $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)<\infty$ one has
$-\frac1t\log L_t=-\frac1t\sum_{n\le t}\log R(X_n)\to\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$
$\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s.\ by the strong law, so \Cref{ass:spectrum} holds with
$D=\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$ and \Cref{prp:stein-gen} contains \Cref{prp:stein-ceiling}.
Under \Cref{ass:homog} and provided $\mathbb{P}_0(L_t>0)=1$ for every $t$ ---
equivalently $\lambda_n(0^{+})<\infty$ for every $n$, so that
$\log L_t=\sum_{n\le t}\log R_n$ $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s.\ --- the quantity
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[-\log R_n]$ need not be constant in $n$, and $D$ is then the limit
of $\frac1t\sum_{n\le t}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[-\log R_n]$ whenever a weak law applies.
<!-- end remark-36 -->
<!-- lemma-27: body_md -->
\label{lem:compensator}
Fix $t\in\mathbb{N}$ and assume $\lambda_n(0^{+})<\infty$ $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s.\ for every
$n\le t$, so that $\mathbb{P}_0(L_t>0)=1$. Then $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s.
\[
   -\log L_t\ =\ A_t+M_t ,\qquad
   A_t:=\sum_{n\le t}\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_n ,\qquad
   M_t:=\sum_{n\le t}\left(-\log R_n-\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_n\right) ,
\]
with $(A_t)$ predictable and nondecreasing and $(M_t)$ a $\mathbb{P}_0$-martingale
with $M_0=0$; and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ceiling-is-divergence}
   \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}\left[\frac{A_t}{t}\right]
   \ =\ \frac1t\,\mathrm{KL}\left(\mathbb{P}_0|_{\mathcal{F}_t}\,\big\|\,\mathbb{P}_1|_{\mathcal{F}_t}\right) .
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-27 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
$\log L_t=\sum_{n\le t}\log R_n$ $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s.\ on $\left\{ L_t>0\right\}$, and
$\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_n=-\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[\log R_n\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]\in[0,\infty)$ by
\Cref{lem:limit-cond}; this is the Doob decomposition. Taking
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}$ and using $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[M_t]=0$ gives
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[A_t]=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[-\log L_t]
=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[\log\frac{d\mathbb{P}_0|_{\mathcal{F}_t}}{d\mathbb{P}_1|_{\mathcal{F}_t}}]$.
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prp:rate}
Assume $\lambda_n(0^{+})<\infty$ $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s.\ and
$\operatorname{Var}_{\mathbb{P}_0}(\log R_n\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1})\le \bar v<\infty$ $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s.\ for
every $n$. Then $\frac1tM_t\to0$ $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s., so that
$\frac1tA_t$ and $-\frac1t\log L_t$ have the same limits: for
$D\in[0,\infty)$,
\[
   \frac1t\sum_{n\le t}\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_n\ \xrightarrow[t\to\infty]{}\ D
   \quad\mathbb{P}_0\text{-a.s.}
   \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
   -\frac1t\log L_t\ \xrightarrow[t\to\infty]{}\ D
   \quad\mathbb{P}_0\text{-a.s.}
\]
In that case \Cref{ass:spectrum} holds with this $D$, and under
\Cref{ass:homog} the ceiling $\frac1t\sum_{n\le t}\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_n$ of
\Cref{thm:ceiling-gen} converges to the exponent $D$ of \Cref{prp:stein-gen}.
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
The increments $\Delta M_n=-\log R_n-\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_n$ are $\mathbb{P}_0$-martingale
differences with $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[(\Delta M_n)^{2}]\le\bar v$, so the argument of
\Cref{prp:powerone-gen} --- with $\mathbb{P}_1$ replaced by $\mathbb{P}_0$ and $\log E_n$
by $-\log R_n$ --- gives $\frac1tM_t\to0$ $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s. The equivalence and the
last two claims follow from \Cref{lem:compensator}, a.s.\ convergence implying
convergence in probability.
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- remark-37: body_md -->
\label{rem:rate}
Whether the limit exists at all depends on the model.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),leftmargin=2.4em]
\item \emph{The i.i.d.\ model.} $\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_n=\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$ for every $n$
      (\Cref{lem:limit-cond}), so $D=\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)$ and the ceiling does not
      depend on the horizon. This is why \Cref{sec:ceiling} states one number.
\item \emph{Independent, not identically distributed.} Under \Cref{ass:homog}
      the average is the Ces\`aro mean of the deterministic sequence
      $\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_n$, which need not converge. Let
      $\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_n=1$ for $n\in[2^{2k},2^{2k+1})$ and $\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_n=0$ for
      $n\in[2^{2k+1},2^{2k+2})$, $k\in\mathbb{N}_0$. Then
      $\frac1t\sum_{n\le t}\overline{\mathrm{KL}}_n$ has $\liminf=\frac13$ and
      $\limsup=\frac23$. The ceiling is then genuinely a function of the
      horizon, and \Cref{thm:ceiling-gen} is the only form available.
\item \emph{Stationary ergodic.} If $\mathbb{P}_0$ is stationary and ergodic and
      $\mathbb{P}_1$ is a stationary Markov measure of finite order, then
      $-\frac1t\log L_t$ converges $\mathbb{P}_0$-a.s.\ to the relative entropy rate
      $\bar D(\mathbb{P}_0\|\mathbb{P}_1)
      =\lim_t\frac1t\mathrm{KL}(\mathbb{P}_0|_{\mathcal{F}_t}\|\mathbb{P}_1|_{\mathcal{F}_t})$, by the generalised
      Shannon--McMillan--Breiman theorem \cite{Bar85}, \cite{AC88}. By
      \Cref{prp:rate} the ceiling converges to the same value, and
      \eqref{eq:ceiling-is-divergence} identifies it in expectation at every
      finite $t$.
\end{enumerate}
Note the direction: \Cref{ass:standing} constrains
$\mathrm{KL}(\mathbb{P}_1|_{\mathcal{F}_t}\|\mathbb{P}_0|_{\mathcal{F}_t})$, while
\eqref{eq:ceiling-is-divergence} is about
$\mathrm{KL}(\mathbb{P}_0|_{\mathcal{F}_t}\|\mathbb{P}_1|_{\mathcal{F}_t})$ --- the same asymmetry between the two
divergences that \Cref{thm:two} records for the i.i.d.\ model.
<!-- end remark-37 -->
<!-- assumption-4: body_md -->
\label{ass:ge}
With $S_t:=\log W_t$, the limit
$\Psi(\theta):=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac1t\log\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[e^{\theta S_t}]$ exists
in $(-\infty,\infty]$ for every $\theta\in\mathbb{R}$; $0$ lies in the interior of
$\mathcal D_\Psi:=\left\{\theta\;\middle|\;\Psi(\theta)<\infty\right\}$; and $\Psi$ is lower
semicontinuous and essentially smooth on $\operatorname{int}\mathcal D_\Psi$ ---
that is, the hypotheses of \cite[Thm.~2.3.6]{DZ10}. Write
$\Psi^{\star}(x):=\sup_{\theta\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{\theta x-\Psi(\theta)\right\}$.
<!-- end assumption-4 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{prp:exponent-gen}
Assume \Cref{ass:ge}, that $\Psi'(0)>0$, and that $0$ lies in the interior of
$\left\{ x\;\middle|\;\Psi^{\star}(x)<\infty\right\}$. Then, for every $\alpha\in(0,1)$,
\[
   \lim_{t\to\infty}-\frac1t\log\gamma_t(\alpha)
   \ =\ \sup_{s\ge0}\ \lim_{t\to\infty}\Lambda^{(t)}_s
   \ =\ \Psi^{\star}(0) .
\]
Both extra hypotheses are needed: they are the analogues of
$\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[\log E]>0$ and of the interiority hypothesis of \Cref{prp:exponent},
and \Cref{ass:ge} alone does not imply either.
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
\Cref{ass:ge} is the hypothesis of the G\"artner--Ellis theorem
\cite[Thm.~2.3.6]{DZ10} for $(S_t/t)_{t\in\mathbb{N}}$, which therefore satisfies a
large-deviation principle with good convex rate function $\Psi^{\star}$; and
$\Psi^{\star}$ vanishes at $\Psi'(0)>0$, is nonincreasing on
$(-\infty,\Psi'(0)]$, and is continuous at $0$ by the interiority hypothesis.
The argument of \Cref{prp:exponent} now applies with $I=\Psi^{\star}$ and
$\gamma_t(\alpha)=\mathbb{P}_1(S_t/t\le\ell/t)$, giving the first equality. For the
second, $\lim_t\Lambda^{(t)}_s=-\Psi(-s)$ by definition, so
$\sup_{s\ge0}\lim_t\Lambda^{(t)}_s=\sup_{\theta\le0}\{-\Psi(\theta)\}$; and for
$\theta>0$ convexity gives $\Psi(\theta)\ge\Psi(0)+\theta\Psi'(0)>0$, so
$-\Psi(\theta)<0\le-\Psi(0)\le\Psi^{\star}(0)$ and positive $\theta$ do not
contribute to $\Psi^{\star}(0)=\sup_{\theta\in\mathbb{R}}\{-\Psi(\theta)\}$.
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{prp:powerone-gen}
Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a betting sequence with
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[\log E_n\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]\ge c>0$ and
$\operatorname{Var}_{\mathbb{P}_1}(\log E_n\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1})\le v<\infty$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.\ for every
$n$. Then $\tau_\alpha<\infty$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.\ for every $\alpha\in(0,1)$.
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
Put $\Delta_n:=\log E_n-\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[\log E_n\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]$, a square-integrable
$\mathbb{P}_1$-martingale difference sequence. The martingale
$N_t:=\sum_{n\le t}\frac{\Delta_n}{n}$ has
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[N_t^{2}]=\sum_{n\le t}\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_1}[\Delta_n^{2}]}{n^{2}}
\le v\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-2}<\infty$, so $N_t$ converges $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.; Kronecker's
lemma gives $\frac1t\sum_{n\le t}\Delta_n\to0$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s. Hence
$\liminf_t\frac1t\log W_t\ge c>0$ and $\log W_t\to+\infty$ $\mathbb{P}_1$-a.s.
<!-- end proof-52 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:app-ville}
Let $(U_t)_{t\in\mathbb{N}_0}$ be a nonnegative supermartingale on a filtered
probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal{B}_{\Omega},(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t\in\mathbb{N}_0},\mathbb{P})$ with $U_0\le1$
$\mathbb{P}$-a.s. Then for every $x\in(1,\infty)$,
\[
   \mathbb{P}\left(\sup_{t\in\mathbb{N}_0}U_t\ \ge\ x\right)\ \le\ \frac1x .
\]
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{thm:app-holder}
Let $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{X}},\mu)$ be a measure space and let $r,r'\in(1,\infty)$ satisfy
$\frac1r+\frac1{r'}=1$. Then for all measurable $g,h:\mathcal{X}\to[0,\infty]$,
\[
   \int gh\,d\mu\ \le\ \left(\int g^{r}d\mu\right)^{1/r}\left(\int h^{r'}d\mu\right)^{1/r'} ,
\]
with equality if and only if there are constants $c_1,c_2\ge0$, not both zero,
with $c_1g^{r}=c_2h^{r'}$ $\mu$-a.e.; for the ``only if'' direction one needs
$0<\int g^{r}d\mu<\infty$ and $0<\int h^{r'}d\mu<\infty$.
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{cor:app-holder}
Let $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal{F}$ a
sub-$\sigma$-algebra, and $r,r'\in(1,\infty)$ with $\frac1r+\frac1{r'}=1$. Then
for all measurable $G,H:\Omega\to[0,\infty]$,
\[
   \mathbb{E}\left[ GH\mid\mathcal G\right]\ \le\ \left(\mathbb{E}\left[ G^{r}\mid\mathcal G\right]\right)^{1/r}
                            \left(\mathbb{E}\left[ H^{r'}\mid\mathcal G\right]\right)^{1/r'}
   \qquad\mathbb{P}\text{-a.s.}
\]
Write $A:=(\mathbb{E}[G^{r}\mid\mathcal G])^{1/r}$ and
$B:=(\mathbb{E}[H^{r'}\mid\mathcal G])^{1/r'}$. On the $\mathcal G$-measurable event
$\left\{0<A,B<\infty\right\}$, equality holds a.s.\ if and only if
$G^{r}/A^{r}=H^{r'}/B^{r'}$ a.s.
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-53: body_md -->
Write $A:=(\mathbb{E}[G^{r}\mid\mathcal G])^{1/r}$ and $B:=(\mathbb{E}[H^{r'}\mid\mathcal G])^{1/r'}$, both
$\mathcal G$-measurable with values in $[0,\infty]$. On $\left\{ A=0\right\}$ we have $G=0$
a.s.\ conditionally, hence $\mathbb{E}[GH\mid\mathcal G]=0$; likewise on $\left\{ B=0\right\}$; and on
$\left\{ A=\infty\right\}\cup\left\{ B=\infty\right\}$ the right-hand side is $+\infty$ unless the
other factor vanishes, which is the case just treated. So it suffices to argue
on $\mathcal G$-measurable event $\left\{0<A,B<\infty\right\}$. There Young's inequality
$xy\le\frac{x^{r}}{r}+\frac{y^{r'}}{r'}$ applied pointwise to $x=G/A$,
$y=H/B$ and conditioned on $\mathcal G$ gives, using that $A,B$ are $\mathcal G$-measurable,
\[
   \frac{\mathbb{E}[GH\mid\mathcal G]}{AB}
   \ \le\ \frac{\mathbb{E}[G^{r}\mid\mathcal G]}{r\,A^{r}}+\frac{\mathbb{E}[H^{r'}\mid\mathcal G]}{r'\,B^{r'}}
   \ =\ \frac1r+\frac1{r'}\ =\ 1 .
\]
Young's inequality is an equality exactly at $x^{r}=y^{r'}$, so on
$\left\{0<A,B<\infty\right\}$ the displayed inequality is an equality if and only if the
conditional expectation of the nonnegative gap
$\frac{G^{r}}{rA^{r}}+\frac{H^{r'}}{r'B^{r'}}-\frac{GH}{AB}$ vanishes, i.e.\ if
and only if the gap itself vanishes a.s., i.e.\ $G^{r}/A^{r}=H^{r'}/B^{r'}$ a.s.
<!-- end proof-53 -->
<!-- remark-38: body_md -->
\label{rem:app-holder}
\Cref{thm:upper-cond} applies \Cref{cor:app-holder} under
$\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_0}[\,\cdot\mid\mathcal{F}_{n-1}]$ with $r=\frac1{1-\beta}$, $r'=\frac1\beta$,
$G=E_n^{1-\beta}$ and $H=(R_nE_n^{-s})^{\beta}$; no finiteness is needed for the
inequality, and \Cref{prp:equality-cond} checks the proviso of the equality
clause before using it.

\Cref{thm:upper} applies the unconditional \Cref{thm:app-holder} with
$r=\frac{1}{1-\beta}$,
$r'=\frac1\beta$, $g=(p_0E)^{1-\beta}$ and $h=(p_1E^{-s})^{\beta}$, so that
$\int g^{r}d\mu=\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[E]\in(0,1]$ and
$\int h^{r'}d\mu=\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[E^{-s}]\in(0,\infty]$ once the degenerate cases of
Step 1 there are excluded. The inequality itself needs no finiteness. For the
equality case the provisos do hold: if $\mathbb{E}_{P_1}[E^{-s}]=\infty$ then
$\Lambda_s(E)=-\infty<\lambda(\beta)$, so equality forces it to be finite, and
$\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[E]>0$ because $\mathbb{E}_{P_0}[E]=0$ would give $E=0$ $P_0$-a.s.\ and hence
$P_1$-a.s.
<!-- end remark-38 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{thm:app-kolmogorov}
Let $(Y_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be independent real random variables on
$(\Omega,\mathcal{B}_{\Omega},\mathbb{P})$ with $\mathbb{E}[Y_n]=0$ and $\mathbb{E}[Y_n^{2}]<\infty$, and put
$M_n:=\sum_{m\le n}Y_m$. Then for every $t\in\mathbb{N}$ and every $x>0$,
\[
   \mathbb{P}\left(\max_{n\le t}|M_n|\ \ge\ x\right)\ \le\ \frac{\mathbb{E}[M_t^{2}]}{x^{2}} .
\]
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{thm:app-cramer}
Let $(Y_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be i.i.d.\ real random variables on $(\Omega,\mathcal{F}_\infty,\mathbb{P})$
with cumulant generating function $\kappa_Y:\mathbb{R}\to(-\infty,\infty]$,
$\kappa_Y(\theta):=\log\mathbb{E}[e^{\theta Y_1}]$, and let
$\bar Y_t:=t^{-1}\sum_{n\le t}Y_n$. Put
\[
   I:\mathbb{R}\to[0,\infty],\qquad
   I(x):=\sup_{\theta\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{\theta x-\kappa_Y(\theta)\right\} .
\]
Then $(\bar Y_t)_{t\in\mathbb{N}}$ satisfies a large deviation principle with rate
function $I$: for every closed $F\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ and every open $G\subseteq\mathbb{R}$,
\[
   \limsup_{t\to\infty}\tfrac1t\log\mathbb{P}(\bar Y_t\in F)\le-\inf_{x\in F}I(x),
   \qquad
   \liminf_{t\to\infty}\tfrac1t\log\mathbb{P}(\bar Y_t\in G)\ge-\inf_{x\in G}I(x) .
\]
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
\label{thm:app-stein}
Let $X_1,\dots,X_t$ be i.i.d.\ with one-observation law $P_0$ or $P_1$, and let
$\mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)<\infty$. For $\alpha\in(0,1)$ set
\[
   \gamma^{\star}_t(\alpha):=\inf\left\{ P_1^{\otimes t}(C_t)\ :\
      C_t\in\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{X}}^{\otimes t},\ P_0^{\otimes t}(C_t^{c})\le\alpha\right\} ,
\]
the least type-II error of a test with acceptance region $C_t$ for $P_0$ and
type-I error at most $\alpha$. Then
\[
   \lim_{t\to\infty}\ -\frac1t\log\gamma^{\star}_t(\alpha)\ =\ \mathrm{KL}(P_0\|P_1)
   \qquad\text{for every }\alpha\in(0,1) .
\]
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- remark-39: body_md -->
\label{rem:app-stein}
\cite[Thm.~11.8.3]{CT06} proves \Cref{thm:app-stein} for
$\alpha\in(0,\frac12)$; that the value does not change for
$\alpha\in[\frac12,1)$ is the strong converse of \cite{HK89}. It is that
range-free form which \Cref{prp:stein-ceiling} uses, since nothing in this
paper restricts $\alpha$ below $\frac12$. (\cite{CT06} constrain the type-I
error by $<\alpha$ rather than $\le\alpha$; the exponent is the same for every
$\alpha\in(0,1)$, so the difference is immaterial.)
<!-- end remark-39 -->
<!-- theorem-14: body_md -->
\label{thm:app-renyi}
Let $Q,P$ be probability measures on $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{X}})$ and let $\mathrm{D}_a$ be as in
\Cref{def:renyi}; no absolute continuity is assumed. Then, for $a\in(0,1)$,
\[
   \mathrm{D}_a(Q\|P)=\frac{a}{1-a}\,\mathrm{D}_{1-a}(P\|Q) ;
\]
the map $a\mapsto\mathrm{D}_a(Q\|P)$ is nondecreasing on $(0,1)$; and
$\lim_{a\uparrow1}\mathrm{D}_a(Q\|P)=\mathrm{KL}(Q\|P)$, with no further hypothesis. (The
proviso ``$\mathrm{KL}(Q\|P)=\infty$ or $\mathrm{D}_b(Q\|P)<\infty$ for some $b>1$'' in
\cite{vEH14} governs the two-sided limit at order one, not the left limit used
here.)
<!-- end theorem-14 -->
<!-- remark-40: body_md -->
\label{rem:app-renyi}
By \Cref{lem:Zf}(iii), $\lambda(\beta)=\mathrm{D}_{1-\beta}(P_0\|P_1)$, so
\Cref{lem:Zf}(ii) and \Cref{lem:limit} are instances of the monotonicity and
the limit above, and \Cref{lem:Zf}(iii) itself is the skew-symmetry identity.
We proved all three directly in \Cref{sec:ceiling} to keep the argument
self-contained.
<!-- end remark-40 -->
<!-- theorem-15: body_md -->
\label{thm:app-variational}
Let $a\in(0,1)$ and let $Q,P$ be probability measures on $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{X}})$ with
$Q\ll P$. Then, with $\mathrm{D}_a$ as in \Cref{def:renyi},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:app-variational}
   \mathrm{D}_a(Q\|P)\ =\ \inf_{\mu\ll Q}
   \left\{\ \mathrm{KL}(\mu\|P)\ +\ \frac{a}{1-a}\,\mathrm{KL}(\mu\|Q)\ \right\} ,
\end{equation}
the infimum running over probability measures $\mu$ on $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{X}})$ and
being attained at the measure $\mu_a$ with
$\frac{d\mu_a}{dP}\propto\left(\frac{dQ}{dP}\right)^{a}$.
<!-- end theorem-15 -->
<!-- remark-41: body_md -->
\label{rem:app-variational}
Put $a=1-\beta$ and $s=\frac{1-\beta}{\beta}$, so that $\frac{a}{1-a}=s$, and
take $Q=P_0$, $P=P_1$. Then \eqref{eq:app-variational} reads
\begin{equation}\label{eq:lambda-inf}
   \lambda(\beta)\ =\ \mathrm{D}_{1-\beta}(P_0\|P_1)
   \ =\ \inf_{\mu\ll P_0}\left\{\ \mathrm{KL}(\mu\|P_1)+s\,\mathrm{KL}(\mu\|P_0)\ \right\} ,
\end{equation}
attained at the $\mu$ with $\frac{d\mu}{dP_0}=R_\beta=\frac{R^{\beta}}{Z_\beta}$,
while \Cref{thm:upper} together with \Cref{lem:flat} reads
\begin{equation}\label{eq:lambda-sup}
   \lambda(\beta)\ =\ \sup_{E\in\mathcal{E}}\ \left\{-\log\mathbb{E}_{P_1}\left[ E^{-s}\right]\right\}
   \ =\ \sup_{E\in\mathcal{E}}\ \Lambda_s(E) ,
\end{equation}
attained at $E=R_\beta$. The two are convex duals: \eqref{eq:lambda-inf} is an
infimum over \emph{measures} of a weighted pair of Kullback--Leibler
divergences, \eqref{eq:lambda-sup} a supremum over \emph{\textsf{e}-variables{}} of a
log-moment, and the same $R_\beta$ solves both --- as a density in the first and
as a test function in the second. What \Cref{sec:ceiling} adds to
\eqref{eq:lambda-inf} is \eqref{eq:lambda-sup}: the constraint set is exactly
$\mathcal{E}$, so the value is exactly the largest tilted exponent available at tilt
$\beta$, and by \Cref{prp:upper-seq} the same bound survives conditioning, hence
holds for every test supermartingale{}.

The companion duality in the opposite direction --- a variational formula for
an exponential integral in which a R\'enyi divergence appears as the penalty
rather than as the value --- is \cite[Thm.~2.1]{ACD15}: for real
$\beta'<\gamma'$, both nonzero, and bounded measurable $g:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}$,
\[
   \frac1{\beta'}\log\int e^{\beta' g}\,d\nu
   \ =\ \inf_{\theta}\left\{\frac1{\gamma'}\log\int e^{\gamma' g}\,d\theta
      +\frac1{\gamma'}\,\mathrm{D}_{\gamma'/(\gamma'-\beta')}(\nu\|\theta)\right\} ,
\]
the infimum over probability measures $\theta$ on $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{X}})$. Here the
order $a=\gamma'/(\gamma'-\beta')$ lies outside $(0,1)$; the formula
$\mathrm{D}_a(Q\|P)=\frac{1}{a-1}\log\int q^{a}p^{1-a}d\mu$ of \Cref{def:renyi}
defines $\mathrm{D}_a$ for every $a\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0,1\}$ and is what is meant. The
coefficient $\frac1{\gamma'}$ is $\frac{1}{\gamma'-\beta'}$ in the normalisation
$\frac{1}{a(a-1)}\log\int q^{a}p^{1-a}d\mu$ used in \cite{ACD15}, and likewise
\Cref{thm:app-variational} is \cite[Thm.~1]{Ana18} rescaled by
$\mathrm{D}_a=a\,R_a$.
<!-- end remark-41 -->
